utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Full name, please.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I am General Roderick Cordy-Simpson, a recently retired Lieutenant-General from the British army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Having been a soldier in the British army for some 31-plus years --

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I was 35 years in the army when I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Appointed chief of staff of UNPROFOR's Bosnia-Herzegovinan command on the 18th of September, 1992, working under General Philip Morillon until the 10th of April of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your principal task being to implement the military direction given by General Morillon for the whole of Bosnia, thus freeing him to devote himself more to political matters?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 29th of October, 1992, were you stationed in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Starting in the beginning of November 1992, did you organise meetings called the Mixed Military Working Group meetings which brought together the three deputy commanders of the warring factions at Sarajevo Airport?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did that group meet initially a couple of times a week for several hours, although I think later it met more frequently?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: At least once a week initially, sometimes twice a week, but by December, on directions from the United Nations in New York, we went into almost permanent session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Typically, was the group chaired by you and attended by Blaskic, Guervo, and Siber for the three parties?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That's correct, General Guervo, Colonel Blaskic, and Colonel Siber representing the three parties at deputy commander level.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The functions of the group being broadly to deal with ceasefire arrangements, safe routes around Sarajevo and other centres to facilitate access of aid convoys?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your dealings with Blaskic, did you find him to be, first, a military man and, secondly, a man whose word you were able to rely on?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Overall, I found that Colonel Blaskic, as he was then, was a military commander whose word, with one exception, I could trust, and on one occasion, I know that he let me down that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are bundles of documents prepared which can conveniently be placed before the witness, Defence counsel, and the bench, and although they bear separate exhibit numbers, which I will read out for the purposes of the record as the witness refers to them, it will be swifter, I think, if the bundles are presented comprehensively to all parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you been able to review this morning very briefly some minutes of some of the meetings that you've referred to?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I have, very briefly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Document 264.1, dated on sheet one the 1st of November, on sheet two refers to a report of a meeting between General Morillon and Colonel Blaskic on the 19th of October. Was this, in fact, a Mixed Military Working Group meeting or was this a meeting that preceded those meetings?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It was one that preceded the first Mixed Military Working Group and was a bi-party meeting between General Morillon and Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On that same second sheet, on the penultimate paragraph, Colonel Blaskic is recorded as having evidence of a growing infiltration of Mujahedin mercenaries posing as journalists on diplomatic passports, saying that there were some 3.000 to 4.000 of them having joined Muslim fighters and being protected by diplomatic immunity. Was that an allegation that was made from time to time or was it unique to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No. It was a constant theme of the Croat delegation and, I have to say, the Serb delegation as well throughout the conflict while I was there, and although -- and there was clearly some evidence that there were some Muslim fighters from Arabic countries in Bosnia, although I have to say the figure of up to 4.000 was probably -- we had little evidence to bear such a high figure out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Second document, 274.1, the document dated the 10th of November, but on the second sheet recording a meeting held at Sarajevo Airport on the 7th of November, the delegation for the HVO led by Colonel Blaskic, and the third sheet revealing at the opening paragraph 6 that you were introduced by General Morillon as the chairman of the meeting on that date. So does that document accurately date the start of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It accurately reflects the Mixed Military Working Group effectively coming under my chairmanship, except on one or two occasions subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Third document, 279.1, dated the 12th of November but reflecting, on the second sheet, a meeting held on the 10th of November, on the third sheet, one sees at paragraph 7 the HVO representative, we know that they were led by Colonel Blaskic, issuing a verbal process concerning the attacks on Mostar, Travnik, and Jajce but declaring he was authorised to sign any agreement that could bring peace. Did Colonel Blaskic at these meetings come apparently clothed with such authority, General?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: He did, indeed. Furthermore, as a result of that meeting, a ceasefire held for about two weeks throughout the whole of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The third sheet, the following sheet on the document, paragraph 15, the HVO delegation stated that the agreement should be signed by the parties present. If the signature of the Republic of Croatia was required, although not the responsibility for HQ UNPROFOR, the former Yugoslavia and its armed forces should also sign it. Paragraph 20 reads that after the signing of the agreement, the Serb delegation stated that for successful implementation, it was necessary that the Croatian forces withdraw from occupied territories and attempts had to be made to have Croatia sign the agreement. The alleged involvement of external forces and the requirement for external states to be involved in the peace process, was that something that occurred only once or did it recur?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It was a fairly constant theme from both, but particularly from the Serbs throughout, that Croatian regular forces were operating inside Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout the time that I was in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next document, 289.1, dated the 21st of November, the second sheet reflecting a meeting held on the 20th of November, and towards the foot of the page at paragraph 2(a), the following is set out: "Dr. Karadzic showed considerable concern about the Croatian Republic's increasingly open intervention in Bosnia-Herzegovina," and further comments. Two sheets further on, at paragraph 10(a) at the foot of the page, Dr. Karadzic voiced extreme concern about the involvement of the Croatian republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina: "This is an issue we will have to address." General, is this further evidence of the same type that you referred to in your last answer?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next exhibit in time has already been produced and is separate from that bundle. No, it's -- if you leave that one where it was and the Court Deputy will provide you with Exhibit Z297, please, a document that the Chamber has already considered. Does this document, General, fit in the sequence of the reports of your meetings, this document relating to a meeting on the 28th of November, where at paragraph 5 in the opening this is recorded: "All delegations were present and welcomed by the chairman. Colonel Kordic was the new chairman of the HVO delegation. He introduced himself as the superior of Colonel Blaskic and stated that he would be in attendance at all future MMW meetings. All delegations agreed to the fact that an U.N. television team would film the opening of the meeting." From this moment on, what was Colonel Kordic's role in the meetings?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Colonel Kordic, from here on in, was the senior representative at the HVO at all Mixed Military Working Groups and, therefore, was -- effectively had become the deputy commander of the HVO as far as the HVO were concerned, and he was accepted as such by General Guervo, the deputy commander of the Bosnian Serbs, and Colonel Siber, the deputy commander of what in those days was known as the Presidency Forces, i.e., the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we turn to the fifth sheet of this particular document, paragraph 27, "Atmosphere," and the anti-penultimate line of that paragraph: "During this meeting it was assessed that Colonel Kordic will participate actively." And for the first time it was assessed that the chairman would be able to build a relationship with Major Guervo. So that was your immediate assessment of Colonel Kordic?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is correct. I found him, at this stage, cooperative and clearly the leader of the HVO delegation with responsibilities that went with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next document from the bundle, please, 306.1, is a letter dated the 7th of December, but tell us first, please, General, was there a meeting of the group held on or about that day?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, there had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who had attended?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: General Guervo and Colonel Siber. The HVO delegation had not attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This letter arrived by what means?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It was faxed into our headquarters in Kiseljak on the morning of the meeting itself, stating that the HVO would be unable to attend the meeting. I had left the headquarters by then to attend, to chair the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The letter reads, so far as material, in the first substantive paragraph: "Respecting the super-human efforts of UNPROFOR and your personal efforts for stopping the war in BH, when you already have and will have the full support of the Croatian people in your humanitarian mission in the future, the HVO delegation estimates that at this time the minimal conditions for the resuming of tripartite negotiations of military delegations are interrupted. We propose the cancellation of the meeting unless minimal conditions for negotiations are met with." In the following paragraph he sets out alleged harassment, and the following paragraph proposes a new place for negotiations, in the penultimate paragraph that negotiations take place in the Hotel Dalmatia in Kiseljak, and in the last paragraph a written guarantee of the highest military level of each delegation on the security of military delegations through zones of responsibility, that letter then being signed by Colonel Dario Kordic. Can you help us please? What was the effect of this document being faxed at the time it was faxed?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: The first thing was, of course, that the meeting of the Mixed Military Working Group was effectively fruitless because the Serbs and the Bosniaks, the Presidency Forces, refused to sit at the table with each other without the third member being present, i.e., the HVO, so it was a meeting that, frankly, was of little great consequence on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next document, please, Z314, is a document dated the 14th of December, but to deal with things chronologically we must go first to the last two sheets, to a minute dated the 13th of December, reflecting a meeting held on the 12th of December. Is the position that there was a meeting between you and Colonel Kordic at your base in Kiseljak on the 12th of December?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Planned or unplanned?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Unplanned. Colonel Kordic came to see me at very short notice, really to explain his non-attendance at the previous Mixed Military Working Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I suspect at some stage the Chamber will want to read this document in full. It will take a minute or so to read it out, but it's probably wiser if I do that, unless the Court prefer to read it to itself. It's two sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The last two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us look at it. Yes, we've read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last paragraph summarises your views, where you set out that his position was not hard and in many ways quite realistic. "Whilst he believed there was some room for manoeuvre in finding a solution to the problems, he was not so hopeful that a solution to the problem of Sarajevo could be found." You agree he would make no statement to the press about the meeting, and expressed the view at that time that he was a highly intellectual and capable journalist-cum-politician, who wielded power and was clearly respected by his side, it being refreshing that he dismissed his minders from the meeting, keeping only a secretary with him. That was your then view of him, was it, General?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That clearly reflects my view of Colonel Kordic at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you understand his attitude to be in general but, in particular, towards the state of Herceg-Bosna and so on?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I think one must remember that at this time, the Serbs were -- at this exact time, the Serbs were putting in a major attack through the suburbs of Otes and Stup in Sarajevo, and there were considerable casualties, not least a large number of Croat personnel who lived in the city had been displaced. It was clearly his concern at this stage to try and do anything he could using the offices of UNPROFOR for the benefit of the Croats, who were effectively refugees now in the middle of Sarajevo itself, in other words, surrounded by the Serbs in a Muslim enclave is what it had become. So that was the first thing. The second point, he was obviously apologising for his non-attendance at the previous meeting. That was partly to do with the fact that there was severe fighting going on at the time in Sarajevo and would account for the fact that he wanted the venue changed in future to somewhere in Kiseljak, which, of course, was totally unacceptable to the Serbs. The protection of himself moving in and out of Sarajevo to the Mixed Military Working Group, I can understand his feelings at that stage. He had been subjected to an unpleasant incident on the return from a Mixed Military Working Group about a week before, where the Serbs had stopped the vehicle in which he was travelling with Colonel Blaskic at night, and although they did not know who was inside the vehicle, and it was subject to considerable bravery of a young Danish second-lieutenant who refused access until I came on the scene, probably at 8.00 at night, and there was potentially a very ugly scene which I managed to defuse, but it must have been of considerable concern to the HVO delegation in the back of a U.N. armoured personnel carrier to know that there was an angry Serb military crowd outside his vehicle. So my opinion of him at this stage was that he was working for the benefits of the Croats. His long-term view was to preserve the potential state of Herceg-Bosna and, in particular, what was in danger of becoming an island in the centre of Bosnia of Cantons 8 and 10, i.e., the central Croat populated area surrounded by a Muslim area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we come back to the beginning of this document to understand its form, we see that the first sheet is dated the 14th of December and that there then follows the minute for the meeting on the 13th of December which was attended by Colonel Kordic, leading the HVO delegation?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And his contributions to the meeting are set out there, and I needn't go through them. The next document, please, is 328.1, dated the 22nd of December. The summary is wrong. That's the cover sheet. The second sheet details a meeting on the 18th of December where the HVO delegation was led by Colonel Kordic. The meeting was addressed by Lord Owen, amongst others, and at the foot of that sheet, we can see that Lord Owen announced a meeting at a higher level in Geneva on the 2nd of January, involving President Izetbegovic, Dr. Karadzic, and Mr. Boban. Over to the following sheet, one observes that this was Colonel Kordic's contribution at 7(a), accepting in general terms the agreement, saying that "As a sign of goodwill of all sides present it is proposed that as a first step we arrange for the freedom of movement of 500 women, children and elderly prior to Christmas." Any comments you want to make on that or not?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Only to say that that clearly, if my memory reflects correctly, refers again to the people who were -- the Croats who were stuck in Sarajevo who Colonel Kordic was trying to get out of Sarajevo and using Christmas as a convenient way of so doing. Of course, it was stopped by the Serbs, who were demanding the free access of 25.000 Serbs in return to move. So I regret it was a stillborn suggestion. It did not come to fruition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last document of the bundle, 336.1, dated the 29th of December, reflecting a meeting on the 22nd of December where the HVO delegation was led by General Petkovic, the other delegation similarly being represented by top-level personnel. If we turn to the next sheet, the third sheet, paragraph 7, was General Petkovic recorded as saying that the agreements as proposed would be signed and that Colonel Kordic would provide the representatives required? Any comment on that? What does that reflect as to Colonel Kordic's role and chain of command?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I took it to reflect that Colonel Kordic had the authority directly from General Petkovic, who was the overall Croat commander, so therefore he was superior to Colonel Blaskic in the official military chain of command and, since he was also a politician, showed really that he wielded considerable influence, both militarily and politically, and particularly in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've dealt already with his having been a journalist. Was there any evidence of his having been a soldier before the war?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: None that I was aware of. In fact, I would suggest he was quite open that he had not been a soldier prior to the conflict in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When he travelled, how did he travel and with what supporters?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Certainly the first time I met him, I mean, obviously at the Mixed Military Working Groups, he travelled under my authority in a U.N. armoured personnel carrier as part of a flag of truce, which was agreed with the Serbs and the Bosniaks, but when he came to my headquarters, I remember clearly, strangely enough, he arrived in a large black Mercedes with a small entourage of sunglass-wearing bodyguards with him. I was quite surprised, as a soldier, that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of your dealings with him, what was your judgement of your ability to rely on his word? You've told us about Blaskic. What about Colonel Kordic?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I would be open that initially I trusted his judgement and his word, but as the situation in Bosnia changed and the breakdown of the uneasy alliance between the Bosniaks and the Croats, particularly in Central Bosnia, happened, I began to form the impression that I could trust his word less and that he was more intent on preserving the Croat influence in Central Bosnia than looking for any long-term, overall political solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll return to that topic the question after next, but can you help us immediately with this: Petkovic and Boban, to what extent were they occupied or, indeed, preoccupied at this time with events outside Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: At this stage, the area of Mostar in particular was under considerable attack by the Serbs, and at the same time, the alliance between the Croats and the Bosniaks had virtually broken down in that area. This had effect that Boban and Petkovic were very much orientated in their requirements to be present in and direct operations in the Mostar area and were able to exercise less time and, therefore, less influence in Central Bosnia. I, therefore, formed the impression that Kordic exercised considerable autonomy with the authority of Petkovic and Boban in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Returning to your trust in him, did you form a view at some stage about the extremity or otherwise of the views he held and their compatibility with the general search for compromise and peace?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I slowly formed the impression that he was more interested in safeguarding the pure Croat influence in Central Bosnia, that he was not genuinely or as interested as he pretended to be in maintaining a sensible alliance against the Serbs at that stage. I recall one incident when I could not get any movement on a particular area at the Mixed Military Working Group between the Serbs and the Bosniaks when Sarajevo was under intense shelling, and so I sent the delegates to their separate rooms and I thought that I might be able to get some form of compromise if I could find the right lever to use, and I asked the view of Colonel Kordic. He slightly surprised me by pointing to an area on the map of Sarajevo which he said that I should persuade the Bosniaks to give up. Now, at this stage, the Bosniaks inside Sarajevo were taking an immense pounding, and I was surprised that he would suggest they give up even more territory if he genuinely believed that we were searching for some form of peace in that area. Of course, when I went back and checked the area, I found that it was the type of area that the Bosniaks could never possibly have been expected to sign up. It would have given away important areas of land overlooking the centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you form a view about why he had the rank of full Colonel accorded to him?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I can only assume that he had taken the rank of full Colonel, that he was of equal status of military hierarchy with Colonel Blaskic who was, up till then, the senior military commander in Central Bosnia. If he had called himself a Lieutenant-Colonel or Major, he would have been junior. Therefore, militarily, not necessarily political, but he would have been junior to Colonel Blaskic. Therefore, he had to have a rank that was of equal rank at least with the military commander in Central Bosnia, Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A couple matters of detail. I think you travelled regularly from Kiseljak to Sarajevo and you spent one day a week in Vitez, and at the beginning of 1993 you visited Maglaj where the ABiH and the HVO were fighting along the same lines, under shared command, something that continued until March 1993?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. They were surrounded by the Serbs at the time and taking a fairly viscous pounding in that town, and it was almost impossible for the U.N. to get in to do anything to help them, but I went in and assessed that the two commanders on the ground, the ABiH and the HVO, were jointly -- and they were sharing a joint command post, were jointly doing an excellent job defending the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 26th of January of 1993, were you present at a meeting with Colonel Stewart in Kiseljak where a ceasefire between the HVO and the ABiH was arranged, the parties represented by Blaskic and Merdan?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is correct. The whole of Central Bosnia had degenerated into ethnic cleansing, torching of houses, and a complete breakdown of law and order, and the blocking and the cutting of the road by the ABiH in a little village called Kacuni, between myself and Colonel Stewart, we forced the road open and then got Blaskic and Merdan to my headquarters in Kiseljak to try and get a ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the point of signing, what happened?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: A rather strange almost pantomime performance took place. As Blaskic was about to sign, his political advisor burst into the room and announced that Busovaca was being attacked and that Croat civilians were being murdered by Mujahedin. Blaskic said he could not, therefore, sign the document and would have to immediately go and investigate. I did, however, force him to return subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you carry out your inquiries as to whether there was truth in what was being said about events in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had a Dutch transport company there and I immediately got in touch with them, who confirmed that Busovaca was completely quiet at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know the name of or can you give any description of the person you describe as the political advisor?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I regret to say I can't remember his name now. He wore a uniform, slightly strangely. He clearly was no form of soldier but exerted considerable influence over Colonel Blaskic, and always used to -- when Blaskic used to attend the Mix Military Working Group in the early days, would attend alongside him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your judgement of this intervention by him bringing incorrect information about Busovaca being that that it was what?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: A deliberate attempt to stall the process that was going on at that period in Geneva. Boban or Karadzic and Izetbegovic were at this very moment in Geneva under Lord Owen's direction, trying to find a peace plan that would be acceptable to all three parties. I felt that it was probably a case of while the rest of the world was seeing Serb and Muslim fighting, to let it also be known that there was considerable fighting against the Croats, particularly in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Blaskic return the following day and was his political advisor with him?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Blaskic did return the following day. However, I ensured that his political advisor was not present, and I purely dealt with Merdan and Blaskic without his political advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened on this day when there was any prospect of an agreement?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I had instructed the Danish guards that no one but no one was allowed to come in or out of the headquarters while I was having the discussions. I got the agreement signed by Blaskic and Merdan. I then stuck them both in front of the world's television cameras to say they had agreed to a ceasefire, and a couple of minutes later a rather harassed political advisor arrived to say that Busovaca was in flames, as was Fojnica. I, fortunately, was able to ring up the Dutch transport company again, who said that all was quiet in Busovaca, and Brigadier Cumming had just come in from Fojnica and was able to tell me that it was a quiet market day in Fojnica and there was nothing untoward going on there whatsoever. At the same time, Mate Boban was announcing in Geneva that Fojnica was in flames.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Give me one minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, in connection with this incident, which occurred apparently twice, to prevent Colonel Blaskic from signing the agreement which was proposed by General Cordy-Simpson, could we learn from the witness if, according to his knowledge, this reflects a disagreement between Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic? Was that the result of a disagreement in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It is a very fair question, and I regret to say I cannot answer it as I have no feel at all about where the direction for what was obviously a well-orchestrated plan was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The plan, as you inferred it to be, was to do what?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I think to show in Geneva that as the peace plan -- the peace plan as suggested by Lord Owen was moving forward, that the importance of the integrity of cantons 8 and 10, i.e., Central Bosnia, was all-important to the Croats, who were -- effectively now would be an island surrounded by Serbs to the north and Muslims both to the east and to the west, and that before they would be prepared to sign it the world had to know that their security in Central Bosnia was threatened. That is my only reading of why this slightly bizarre incident took place. At the same time, Belgrade radio was also stating that Mujahedin were attacking into Kiseljak, which was where I was sitting and could confirm that they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we leave that meeting, the presence or absence of this political secretary or however you describe him, representative, if you would think back to that, and if there's no objection and you would wish to refresh your memory from your statement, if you could do that if necessary, on the second meeting. Can you remember more about it?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Can I refresh my memory from the statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can he be provided with the actual statement? Mine is unmarked. It's unmarked save for one marginal line that is of no significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it's the top of the page you're looking at or possibly the foot of the preceding page.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I -- yes. The political commissar was present on that second day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did he actually do that you noticed as the time passed?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. He was slightly anxiously, looking at his watch as if there was some prearranged time that the messenger would arrive with this, saying Busovaca is in flames, et cetera. He was clearly waiting for someone to burst into -- I got the impression to burst into the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 15 of the summary. After the announcement of the Vance-Owen Plan on the 25th of January, what happened generally so far as fighting is concerned?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: The situation broke down dramatically, particularly in Central Bosnia, particularly in the area of Gornji Vakuf, all up the Lasva Valley. There was considerable fighting. It became extraordinarily difficult to move around in Central Bosnia. Aid conveys into Sarajevo that came down that way were almost exclusively unable to move. Midwinter and Sarajevo was effectively cut off with the airlift no longer happening because of appalling weather and no aid being able to get in down the routes into Sarajevo or into the warehouses in Kiseljak either. A general breakdown in the somewhat shaky alliance that had held up till then between the ABiH and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you, on the 1st of February, convene a meeting --

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- involving the commanders of the 1st and 3rd Corps of the ABiH, together with Blaskic and Kordic, the meeting taking place in Vitez, being chaired by General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I brought the four of them together at Colonel Stewart's, the battalion commander's headquarters, to try and find a way to agree a ceasefire in a situation that was rapidly spinning out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A ceasefire agreement was reached?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did it hold, and if so, to what genuine or what public degree, for some time?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It held effectively until about the 16th of April, which was one of the longest ceasefires that we managed to achieve. Of course, it was a biparty ceasefire and didn't involve the Serbs. But in Central Bosnia the fighting ceased, although the situation remained incredibly tense, with a number of illegal checkpoints and the two lines very firmly drawn with the U.N. trying to persuade both the ABiH and the HVO to pull back from their positions and create a separation of forces, but the ceasefire did hold. Blaskic and Kordic, as the ABiH commanders, were good to their word and delivered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your conclusions from that about their control over the HVO in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It was quite clear that what they had signed at that meeting they were able to deliver insofar as the fighting died down. And although we had isolated incidents of burning of houses and shootings, the large-scale attacks that had been going on prior to this ceased. Therefore, my conclusions were that Kordic and Blaskic, between them, were able to exercise the necessary influence over the military forces in Central Bosnia, as was the 1st and the 3rd Corps commanders of the ABiH over their forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two matters of detail: From the time you knew him, where was Kordic's headquarters, what were they like, and how did they compare with the base of Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Blaskic lived in Kiseljak in the HVO barracks, about 300, 400 metres from where I had my headquarters. Colonel Kordic, if my memory is correct, had his headquarters based in a hotel just before one got to Busovaca on the way north from Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was controlling the power stations and the telephone lines at the time that you were involved?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: In the area of Central Bosnia, they were definitely under the control of the Croats and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the HVO have their own radio station?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: In Kiseljak, its transmitter was. We used to use it quite a lot in order to try and get messages to the population, but, of course, it was strictly controlled and monitored by the HVO as to what we could or couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The position of Blaskic and his political associate, was that something reflected more generally?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No. My initial reaction was that this was some form of political commissar that stood alongside a military commander. However, Colonel Kordic, when he assumed the role in Central Bosnia, did not seem to need to have that type of political advice and control alongside him and seemed to be much more able to make his own political and military decisions without the advice of someone standing right beside him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What you saw with Blaskic, forget Kordic, did you see it with any other personalities in the area at the time?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Not to the same extent, no. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only two other things. Your tour of duty ended in the middle of April of 1993, but you returned to the area since then, and perhaps you can just give us the years of your return and the role you performed there?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. When I left Bosnia in 1993, I spent three months setting up the no-fly zone on behalf of the U.N. in northern Italy with NATO. I then went back and was chief of staff of the British army of the Rhine and commanded the 1st Armoured Division in Germany. Then I returned in late 1996, beginning of November 1996, to Bosnia as the deputy commander and director of operations of the NATO force, stabilisation force, and I remained there until I left in December 1997, just over a year later, when I returned to the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Since retirement from the army, you had or you have several employments, including, in the Kosovo incident, writing for a newspaper, I think?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, amongst a number of mostly charitable works that I deal with now and one consultancy, I have been writing throughout the Kosovo crisis for one of our national newspapers as a military correspondent/analyst.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That concludes my examination-in-chief of this witness, but could all parties please, however, correct one exhibit number? It's the penultimate document in the bundle. It's numbered 328.1. Can it be correctly renumbered 328.2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, are you cross-examining?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Stephen Sayers, and I represent Dario Kordic. General, as I understand it, you were the chief of staff of the Bosnia-Herzegovina command of UNPROFOR from September the 18th, 1992 until the time that you left Bosnia-Herzegovina on April the 10th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I understand that you arrived in Kiseljak to set up the UNPROFOR headquarters on October the 29th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Upon your arrival in Central Bosnia and the Sarajevo area, sir, would it be fair to say that you were confronted by a confusing, complex civil war involving at least three identifiable ethnic factions?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it also be fair to say, in your experience, that this was one of the most chaotic political and military situations that you had encountered in your 31 years at that time of military service in the British army?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. Without a doubt, that was the most chaotic military situation that I had ever faced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: General, please forgive my halting delivery, but you and I speak the same language and I am ashamed to admit that I have been regularly excoriated for speaking too quickly for the interpreters, so it's necessary to have a break between question and answer, if that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. When you arrived in Kiseljak, sir, who was the mayor, do you know?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I met the mayor, but I do not recall his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Does the name Josip Boro sound familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: To be honest with you, I can no longer recall the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's fine. Did the HVO have a separate brigade stationed in the town of Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: They had a military force which they called a brigade in Kiseljak, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the commander of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: To my certain knowledge, Colonel Blaskic was the commander of the forces in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, yes, sir. I believe, sir, that according to your statement, which we may as well have marked as an exhibit so that you can refer to it if you wish --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would just like the usher to take this and we'll mark it as an exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D68/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got copies of this, Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Before I ask the specific question, General Cordy-Simpson, do you recognise this statement as a copy of a statement that you gave in July and August 1995 to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that your office had responsibility for negotiating convoy access into other parts of Bosnia across the confrontation lines between the warring ethnic factions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, the headquarters did, of which I was the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. I believe, General, that you delegated the negotiations regarding that matter to your chief of operations and to your chief of convoy operations?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Turning to the Mixed Military Working Group meetings about which you have testified, I believe that the first of these meetings occurred on November the 5th, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: About then. I arrived at the beginning of November, but I couldn't swear on the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The Mixed Military Working Group was set up essentially under your auspices, was it not?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It was an initiative by General Morillon, the force commander, but I was to run it and chair it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: General, was the purpose of this group to provide what was, in effect, the only available forum at that time for discussions between the three principal warring ethnic factions, the Croats, the Muslims or Bosniaks, and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The group was originally intended to bring the deputy commanders of each of the three sides together to engage in a dialogue with the objective of diffusing tension and ultimately arriving in the end, I suppose, at a peace agreement?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Whilst it was under my chairmanship, that would be correct. It had the ability to go up to the force commander level or even Lord Owen level and to bring together a higher level of representation, which on one or two occasions it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Indeed, you testified that Lord Owen did, in fact, attend some of the Mixed Military Working Group meetings when agreements on major initiatives appeared to be close?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I can recall one, if not two occasions when Lord Owen himself came to the Mixed Military Working Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The deputy commander of the Bosnian Serb army, I think you have previously testified, was General Guervo?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is it accurate to say that General Guervo always brought with him a gentleman who functioned in the role of what you've described fairly vividly as a political commissar?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: He also had a political advisor alongside him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The political advisor that General Guervo brought with him was Colonel Tolimir, I think?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That was correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's true, is it not, that General Guervo would always invariably consult with Colonel Tolimir before signing anything?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Almost invariably, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The deputy commander of the Muslim forces with whom you dealt in these MMWG meetings was Colonel Siber?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Stjepan Siber?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Up until December, or late November of 1992 at least, the Croat representative with whom you dealt was Colonel Tihomir Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You have said, General, that you cannot remember the name of the political commissar -- sorry, advisor that Colonel Blaskic could be seen with, but you have stated in your statement that this was a relatively chubby individual who sported sneakers and a rosary and beads and so forth. Does the name Ignac Kostroman sound familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I deeply regret that I can't remember the name of him, but you have given an accurate description of what he dressed and looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He struck you as, most affirmatively, not a soldier?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, General Cordy-Simpson, that after December the 21st, 1992, Mr. Kordic or Colonel Kordic did not attend any further Mixed Military Working Group meetings, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I am trying to refresh my memory on this. Certainly throughout the period of January, when things had broken down, until early February, there was no attendance at the Mixed Military Working Group because the war on three sides was too severe to achieve anything. I cannot recall after the February agreement, which Colonel Kordic attended at a meeting in Vitez, whether he attended a further Mixed Military Working Group meeting, but certainly by that stage, the number of Mixed Military Working Group meetings, when we could convene all three sides, did fall away quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I have not had the opportunity to review these documents before, the ones that were shown to you today and which consist of about 90 pages by my count, but one I would like to point you to is, and I'm afraid I cannot read the number at the top, Z336.1. This is a document dated December 29th, 1992 that relates to Mixed Military Working Group meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, when you come to a convenient moment, we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just deal with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This document deals with two meetings of this group, sir, on the 22nd and 26th of November, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: The one on the 22nd and the 26th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that Mr. Kordic was not in attendance at either of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Well, the first one, certainly, and I'm just refreshing my memory, was one of the higher level ones and, therefore, was chaired by General Morillon, bringing in General Mladic and General Petkovic in this particular incident and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's the point that I wanted to raise. There's a document that actually has a stamp number on it, R0046377, which appears to be an agreement on the separation of forces in the area of the Sarajevo Airport?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This document is signed by Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection that Mr. Kordic was not present, in fact, at this high-level meeting?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: To be honest with you, I can't give you a straight answer on that because I was not present at that one myself, as it was chaired by General Morillon, and I didn't normally attend the same meetings as he did because it normally meant that we had slightly too large a presence at these meetings which, in turn, was not good for a discussion amongst the three sides, in this case, the two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If that would be a convenient point to take a break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: General, do you recognise the name Major David Pinder-Koehnk?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was he the head of public affairs for UNPROFOR in your Kiseljak headquarters?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Not public affairs, no. He was my press spokesman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He actually made some contemporaneous notes regarding the meetings of the MMWG that were attended by Mr. Kordic, and his notes suggest that there were five such meetings. The first was on December the 12th of 1992. Do you have any recollection of being present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: If it was a Mixed Military Working Group with Colonel Kordic present and it was the 12th of December, I was almost certainly in the chair of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And indeed, the minutes of a meeting that you testified about in your direct-examination, the last two pages of Exhibit Z314, do you recall the --

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That was my meeting with Kordic at Kiseljak, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that this gentleman was the vice-president of the HZ-HB, the so-called Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: He introduced himself as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that he was indeed the vice-president or not?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Insofar as that was the way he introduced himself when he came to my headquarters, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know what the functions of the vice-president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna encompassed?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: To be honest with you, the situation throughout, both the political and military at this stage, was so confused throughout Bosnia and there were so many fractional parties that to be certain what the duties of any one particular one was to an outsider, as I was, would not be something that I could swear to in Court, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Lieutenant-Colonel Bob Stewart has written a book called "Broken Lives". I don't know, have you had the opportunity to read it?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I am referred to it on occasions and I have read through it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart made the point that you just made, that there were factions within groups and groups within factions, and: "Without an established order these different elements had created a situation as close to anarchy as I have yet witnessed." That was on page 318 of his book. Would you agree with those observations on the part of Colonel Stewart, sir?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. There was -- it was extremely difficult to find, in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that stage, what each of the various political factions within factions represented, but one at our level only had a clear impression of the overall three dominant factions which, of course, were ethnic at that stage, Croat, Muslim, and Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You have given us some subjective impressions regarding the position in the hierarchy occupied by Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic. Have you seen any documents that would confirm those positions or confirm your views, or would it be fair to say that that's just a subjective impression that you're left with?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: The only -- it is a subjective judgement based on my knowledge of Colonel Kordic, Colonel Blaskic, General Petkovic, and, of course, General Petkovic's statement at the Mixed Military Working Group where he said that his representative was Colonel Kordic for implementing the agreements made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find the reference that you're referring to. It's paragraph 7, I believe, on the third page of Exhibit Z336.1, which says: "General Petkovic signed the two agreements as proposed and stated that Colonel Kordic would provide the representatives required."

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is the statement I was referring to, and that is the only verbal or written statement that has clearly shown that Colonel Kordic, in my opinion, was answerable to General Petkovic in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It would be fair to say though, wouldn't it, sir, that the hierarchy was relatively confused in your view, and you never really gained a clear picture of who answered to whom, what the chain of command was or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I was clear of the overall political top hierarchy between the three sides as they then constituted. I was also clear on the overall top hierarchy within the military of the three sides and their immediate deputies, because they had been introduced as the people who were authorised to sign for their superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know who the president of the HVO was at the time that these negotiations were occurring, sir?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No is the answer to that. As far as I was concerned, General Petkovic was the overall commander of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that, in fact, the president of the HVO was a gentleman by the name of Dr. Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know what position Mr. Boban occupied? I believe that you gave some testimony about Mr. Boban's participation in international negotiations.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Correct. Although I never personally met Mr. Boban, he was the representative of the Bosnian Croats in Geneva at Lord Owen's conference which he held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you understand Mr. Boban to have any official political position within the political hierarchy of the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Insofar as he was the official representative in Geneva of the Bosnian Croats, I assumed that he was the person understood by Lord Owen, the official to be responsible for delivering the peace plan that Lord Owen was currently working on with Mr. Vance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Boban was actually the president of the HZ-HB, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I wouldn't know the various fractional parts of the political setup of the Croats, and I must emphasise that whilst I was trying to run the U.N. military in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the political negotiations were done by General Morillon, with his political advisor, and, of course, Lord Owen at the top level. I very seldom dealt with the political leaders of the three parties in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Turning back to the notes that Major Pinder-Koehnk made, the four other meetings that he records the presence of Mr. Kordic at was a meeting that occurred sometime between December the 12th and the 17th, a meeting on December 17th, and then the last two were on December the 20th and December the 21st. Do you -- I know it's been six years and no one's expected to have photographic recall, and we don't have notes of some of these meetings from the exhibits that the Prosecution has put before you, but generally speaking, do you have a recollection of being present at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: The answer is if Colonel Kordic was present, representing the Bosnian Croats, I was almost certainly present. There was, of course, one before that, on the 28th of November, that I also recall, where Colonel Kordic came for the first time to the Mixed Military Working Group in Sarajevo, because that was the occasion when he was subjected to a Serb harassment on his way out under a flag of truce that night out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That is the incident that you have previously described that required your personal intervention to resolve what could have been a rather tricky situation?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It was fortunate that I decided to return from forward headquarters in Sarajevo to Kiseljak at that time, although it was long after dark, and ran into this incident and would be the reason, in his subsequent meeting with me, of, one, requesting the venue to be changed in the future and his reference to U.N. protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Under the circumstances, General, the request to change the venue was perfectly understandable, was it not?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It was understandable but, of course, was never going to be acceptable to the Bosnian Serbs, and therefore I deemed that I would have to overrule it in order to keep the Mixed Military Working Groups going, provided I could guarantee the security of the HVO delegation, getting them into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the attendance at these meetings in Sarajevo Airport was accompanied by some personal risk on the part of the people who were actually travelling to the airport venue?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. Although I gave them the guarantee of a U.N. protection into Sarajevo and out again, I think it would be fair that there was an element of personal risk, although they were inside an armoured vehicle which was closed down with escorts of another armoured vehicle. But then the whole of Bosnia was of considerable personal risk wherever you went every day, and certainly if you had to cross the demarcation line three times to get to the centre of Sarajevo, we were all under some form of personal risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say also that during your tour of duty, at least, there were occasions where armoured fighting vehicles received hits from rocket-propelled grenades, from automatic weapons fire, and other circumstances where they came under attack from mortar fire and artillery?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Constantly, not only armoured vehicles, very often soft-skinned vehicles also. But I do not recall an occasion when anyone that I was escorting to a Mixed Military Working Group ever came under any form of direct attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There are just a few points I would like to raise in connection with the minutes of the meeting that you prepared, the meeting that occurred on December the 12th, 1992. There's a reference on the second page to illegal trafficking in contraband in a number of areas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have the document in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What number is it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The page number was 00095022.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think it's the last two pages, Your Honour, of Exhibit Z314.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Specifically, sir, I'm referring to the first paragraph on the second page.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you shed some light upon the illegal trafficking that you were aware had been occurring at around this time?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. There was quite a lot of evidence that one of the United Nations battalions in Sarajevo, in this case, the Ukrainians, were coming out of Sarajevo up into the Kiseljak area, which, of course, was not their area of operations as they were responsible for escorting convoys fundamentally from Sarajevo up into the Republika Srpska, or certainly from Mostar into Sarajevo as well, but not into our area of Kiseljak, that they were coming up there and taking substantial amounts of coffee and cigarettes, in particular, back into Sarajevo which was subsequently being traded by them to the inhabitants of Sarajevo. That was the particular reference by Colonel Kordic on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You also summarise, in the last paragraph, an informal discussion that the two of you had, and you make the observation that Mr. Kordic's position was not hard and, in many ways, quite realistic. I wonder if you could just throw some light on those comments, elaborate upon them a little for all of us.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I found it quite refreshing that I was dealing with him effectively on a one-to-one basis, that he did not need any political advice being given to him in order to speak to me. I found him at this stage helpful and genuinely concerned for the fate of the Croats who had been subjected to a very serious attack in the previous days in Sarajevo by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You had no doubt in your mind that the concerns that Mr. Kordic expressed for the welfare of the Croat citizens in this city under siege were genuine; would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That would be correct to say. I considered it a genuine request for help on behalf of fellow Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, if I might trouble you, in connection with the notes that your press secretary prepared. During one of the Mixed Military Working Group meetings, he reflects the HVO position as permitting UNPROFOR to take control of roadblocks. Do you recall any discussion of that particular subject?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Could you just repeat the question because it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. The notes reflect a discussion of blockades, and then the HVO position was "let UNPROFOR take control but obliged to ask what happened with 1.500 individuals before Christmas." The question is: Do you recall any discussion of a suggestion pursuant to which UNPROFOR forces would assume control of roadblocks or checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: What date was that discussion?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It appears to be December the 17th, 1992, sir.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: The answer is I don't. The reason I asked my question was it was certainly when there were many illegal checkpoints in January. When the Croat/ABiH breakdown happened, there was some talk of us replacing the illegal checkpoints that were springing up up the Lasva Valley and Central Bosnia, and in several occasions, we did just that on a temporary basis to defuse the situation. But I regret to say I have no recall in December as to why I would have been in discussions on that particular subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's no reason for regret, General. It was six years ago. One question I would like to ask you in connection with the December the 20th meeting: Major Pinder-Koehnk reflects that Mr. Kordic said that he had consulted with the military and political authorities as to prior suggestions, and those were acceptable to the HVO side. Do you recall any comments made by Mr. Kordic along those lines, to wit, that he had actually consulted higher military and political authorities, discussed proposals that were under consideration, and conveyed acceptance on the part of the Bosnian Croat side?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Not directly, but the Mixed Military Working Group at that stage was mostly to do with trying to achieve freedom of movement around Sarajevo, what was subsequently to become the blue routes, and was implemented under General Rose. That plan was based on the blue routes that we developed at that time. It is quite possible that Colonel Kordic would have given that agreement because it did not directly affect the Croat population in the same way as it did the Muslims inside Sarajevo or the Serbs surrounding it, and therefore it is perfectly possible that he made that statement, although I do not directly recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You also referred, in your direct testimony, to a conversation that you had with Mr. Kordic in which he suggested that part of the city of Sarajevo should be ceded, I gather, to avert the continued conflict that was raging in the city at that time?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't mean to interrupt you, General.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I recall making that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall that the suggestion was actually that part of the city be ceded to United Nations supervision?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It never really got that far. It was my attempt to try and ask Colonel Kordic if he could come up with some form of formula, because I had frankly run out of patience and ideas as to how I might break the deadlock between the Bosniaks and the Serbs to achieve a freedom of movement, particularly for the United Nations, but a freedom of movement around Sarajevo and in and out of Sarajevo. I don't think it went so far as a proposal that the United Nations should take it over. It was, I think, an attempt by Colonel Kordic to pinpoint an area, and I do roughly recall it was the high ground above Otes and Stup, where he believed that I might be able to persuade the Muslim population of Sarajevo to give up some territory as a gesture which, in turn, would help the Serbs agree to the rest of the blue routes that we were trying to negotiate. I subsequently found that it was, when I studied it in any detail, an unrealistic proposal which the Bosniaks would never agree to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that this suggestion that was made did not impress you as a viable military and political solution to the problems that were confronting the warring factions and you as the mediator, if you like, at that time?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It took a matter of a number of minutes to realise that it was not going to be something that I could take as a further negotiating point in any detail with both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The last entry from Major Pinder-Koehnk's contemporaneous notes to which I would like to draw your attention, is an entry made on December the 21st, 1992, sir. Let me just read it to you. It says: "LO fields, sufficient political progress now made to leave mil to mil experts." Do you recall Lord Owen being present at this December the 21st meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It maybe helpful if you show the witness the minutes of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I mean, Lord Owen was in Sarajevo at the time, and he certainly attended one meeting. Whether it was this particular meeting -- I must assume it is, but without the necessary documentation in front of me I wouldn't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, General, we have not been made privy to that documentation and I do not believe that I actually have a copy of the notes of the December the 21st meeting. Perhaps I do, but I did not see it in -- going through these materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's check on it. What is the source of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The source is the notes that Major Pinder-Koehnk made and on which he has given testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And he referred to a meeting on the 21st and at which he says Lord Owen was present. Very well. Mr. Nice, can you help us as to whether you've got any documents as to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't at the moment because I can't track down the Pinder contemporaneous notes. I can't immediately track down the Pinder contemporaneous notes, although, of course, if those are produced in copy for the witness, he can comment on those. As to the 21st of December, itself, we have only, I think, the 18th of December as part of 328.2; the 19th of December, the last part of that; and then I think we pass straight on, in the documents I've been able to produce, to the 22nd of December. In the break, I was handed one other document that we've been able to unearth but that's not the correct date. So the answer is: No, I don't think I can at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can't take that very much further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I have the notes here if you want me to put them on the ELMO and that would be helpful to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any other reference to the note which is going to -- assist the witness in refreshing his memory?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any other point that you want to make about that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Only this question:

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall any comments, General, being made along the lines that sufficient political progress had, in fact, been made by this time to allow the military issues to be dealt with by the military experts?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Not directly. I mean, many politicians often thought that they had made sufficient progress, but reality five years later was that they hadn't. So I regret that six years, seven years later, I can't recall that particular statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That is fine and we will move on. Do you recall the next day, and we do have minutes or notes of this meeting, the one involving General Petkovic, he actually turned up at this meeting, and I believe General Morillon presided and supervised the signature, alas, by just two of the three factions of a ceasefire agreement?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I remember it happened. What I cannot recall now as to whether I was present at that meeting but almost certainly I was probably present at that meeting because there was a lot going on in Sarajevo at that time and there was a lot of fighting going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I would have thought that the minutes of the meeting would have shown whether I was presented on that particular day though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let the witness see Exhibit 336.1.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I may have been present. I'm not certain, to be honest with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Exhibit Z336.1 states that its subject is the MMWG meetings of the 22nd and 26th of December, 1992. Is this a complete document, sir, because it does not appear to have anything related to the December the 26th, 1992 meeting at all?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I'm not even certain what I'm seeing flashed in front of me on the screen at the moment. Sorry, I've got something which I didn't mean to have. Sorry. We're now talking about the document that I've got in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. If you take a look at the first page of this exhibit, under the word "subject" it makes a reference to MMWG meetings of two separate dates, but the attachments to this exhibit only appear to cover one of those meetings. So the question I had, and I don't think it need detain us very long, is this: Is this a complete document or just partial document to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I would be almost certain now that this was the meeting of the 22nd, because I do recall that I chaired a Mixed Military Working Group on the 26th. I quite clearly recall that I must have been one of the few people working on that particular day in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm somewhat confused by your answer. Are you saying that the date December the 22nd is incorrect or --

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No, I'm not. I'm saying that there were two meetings. I cannot recall whether I attended the first one, the one that you're referring to here. I do know I chaired one on the 26th, which is not, I think, attached to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the question is: Do you know whether this is a partial document or a complete document?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I suspect it is therefore, since the cover note says the 22nd and the 26th, it is an incomplete document and is only referring to the meeting of the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. Let me turn away from these documents to some events that occurred in January of 1993. Do I understand that the ABiH launched an offensive in the northern part of the Kiseljak valley that resulted in the cutting off of the main supply route between Busovaca and Kiseljak at the village of Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
