utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And an additional military operation resulted in the supply route between Kiseljak and the town of Kakanj also being cut by ABiH forces as well?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No. That is not totally correct. At Kacuni it was cut by the ABiH, but with difficulty I was able to get myself as far as the road where it was cut in Kacuni from the south, and Colonel Stewart met me from the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I was -- I'm just reading your statement at page 4 that says: "On January 1993, the BiH cut the road from Kiseljak to Kakanj."

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: At Kakanj they cut it. In other words, we couldn't proceed beyond Kacuni. I apologise. Now I'm seeing what you're saying. It is failure to understand pronunciations of terms. The answer is: Yes, at Kakanj it was also cut by the ABiH. So we have a cut on the road running north/south up from Kiseljak up to Busovaca and a cut on the road that runs west/east out of Kiseljak towards Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As a result of the hostilities that broke out in January of 1993, you convened a long meeting in Kiseljak on the 26th of that month to try to stop the escalation of the hostilities between the HVO and the ABiH. Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In attendance at this meeting were Colonel Stewart; correct?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And his opposite number, if you will, the second in command of the 3rd Corps, Colonel Dzemal Merdan?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It was at this meeting that the political advisor first engaged in what you have described as a pantomime, claiming that there had been still events in Busovaca and that the town was in flames?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware, General, that on the 26th of January there had actually been an atrocity committed by the armed forces of the ABiH in the villages of Dusina, Lasva, Nezirovici, and Gusti Grab?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It was subsequently claimed that was the case. Clearly at that stage I was not aware of it, and as I say, it was subsequently claimed that had happened although I have no direct evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever obtain any information that 13 civilians had actually been murdered by elements of the 7th Muslim Brigade and that the HVO negotiator, Zvonko Rajic, had actually been murdered as well in a very gruesome way?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: The answer at that stage is: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This was an item that was extensively televised, General. I don't know whether you made a practice of monitoring local Croatian television programming, but did you ever see broadcast over the airwaves about news stories covering that massacre and showing all of the bodies lined up?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if, General, the usher might show you Exhibit D58/1, which is the only milinfosum that I would like to show to you. This milinfosum is dated January the 29th, 1993, but actually describes the events in Dusina and the murder of various people in that village. Did you actually ever review milinfosums of this variety during the course of performing your duties in your area of operations?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I reviewed a summary of them, but you must remember that there were more than just one battalion in Bosnia at the time. There was the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall reviewing a summary of this milinfosum or this milinfosum itself?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I don't, but again, this reflects very clearly what happened so often in Bosnia, that what we are seeing here is reported speech. It has been claimed that, passed on in a milinfosum by the milinfo officer of 1 Cheshires. So I accept the fact that I didn't -- I do not recall having seen this. It is, of course, again reported speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir. You would agree then that you do not know, one way or the other, whether this atrocity and massacre actually occurred contemporaneously with the negotiations that were being conducted between Colonels Stewart, Blaskic, and Merdan on January the 26th and 27th of 1993?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Whilst I was conducting those meetings with the people you've just mentioned, the answer is: No, I do not know one way or the other for certain whether this atrocity referred to in the milinfosum did or did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you have referred to a ceasefire agreement that was signed in -- either at the end of January or on February the 1st. Let me ask you this question first: Do you recall specifically the date of that ceasefire agreement, whether it was, in fact, at the end of January or, in fact, in February?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It was on the 1st of February, and I can explain why I have such clear memory of the particular date. General Morillon had just put up his fourth star on that morning and left the headquarters to the meeting proudly wearing his fourth star, and it was the 1st of February that he had been promoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This was the first time that he had ventured forth wearing four stars or the stars of a four-star general, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Four-star French general, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Did you accompany him to that --

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No, I did not. I had to set up the meeting and did not accompany him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Kordic did not actually attend that meeting but that it was, in fact, attended by Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That surprises me because the reports back that I had of the meeting, including the agreement that had been agreed, was that Kordic and Blaskic were both present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me show you Exhibit D54/1, if I may. General, is this an accurate copy, as far as you can recall, of the arrangements made for a substantial ceasefire in Central Bosnia between the HVO and the BiH army, bearing a date of January the 30th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I can see no reason why it should not, but as you can well see, this was a much lower level meeting than the one I referred to on the 1st of February. Where General Morillon chaired it, this was chaired at no more than battalion level by Colonel Stewart, Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart, and Jeremy Fleming, who was the director of the ECMM in that particular area of Central Bosnia. This simply laid the groundwork for a meeting that took place, chaired by General Morillon, on the 1st of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know, General, whether that 1st of February meeting actually produced any written agreement that is different from the one that you have before you?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: To be honest with you, all these years later, I can't, but I suspect that this was the basis of what was to be signed up to on the 1st of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name Franjo Nakic as the second in command of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No. The answer to that is I'm afraid I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One followup question on this topic, General: Do you have any recollection of implementing orders, being signed to implement the various obligations contained in this substantial ceasefire agreement?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I don't recollect it, but it's almost certain that my headquarters would have then put out detailed orders, certainly to the 1st Battalion of the Cheshire's Battle Group, as to how this was to be implemented in Central Bosnia, although I'm afraid I can't now recall signing an order implementing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's quite all right, sir. We actually have already exhibited, and I would like the usher to show you now, if that would be convenient, Exhibit D55/1, which I believe is an ECMM collation of the joint implementing orders. Now, General, feel free to look through this exhibit, but I'd just like to represent to you that it consists of a series of orders signed by the commander of the Middle Bosnia HVO Operative Zone, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, and his opposite number, if you will, the commander of the 3rd Corps in Zenica, General Enver Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt -- I can see that, yes, and was negotiated by the EC Monitoring Mission, which was based in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Are there any other implementing orders, of which you are aware, that would have implemented the ceasefire arrangement that you described was reached on February the 1st or is Exhibit D55/1 an accurate collation, if you like, of the implementing orders that carried into effect the ceasefire agreement between the HVO on the one hand and the ABiH on the other?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I have no doubt that it is an accurate agreement -- a reflection of the agreement that was reached, and it was part of our plan that a joint commission between the 1st Battalion of the Cheshire's Battle Group, because it was their area of responsibility, and the ECMM and the two military commanders in the area, the ABiH and the HVO, would be responsible for implementing this particular ceasefire, because clearly it fell into their areas of responsibility. This would have undoubtedly been delegated down by our headquarters to Colonel Stewart in an order down the U.N. chain of command, and this subsequently would have been developed into what we now see as this document here, which came out from the ECMM. So there is another document clearly somewhere of us delegating the authority to implement the ceasefire, which went down the U.N. chain of command to the battle group, the Cheshire's Battle Group. Of course, the ECMM were not under any direct U.N. command, although we liased closely together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that, General. I believe that you are testifying that these orders that you have before you are the implementing orders signed by the military commanders of the respective operative zones carrying into effect the ceasefire agreement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It would appear so, yes. As I say, we have both the ABiH and the HVO signatures to them, Enver and Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Since the orders are signed by the HVO Central Bosnia Operative Zone commander, I would just like to ask you a few questions, it won't take very long, about Colonel Tihomir Blaskic. He told you, I believe, that he was a former prisoner of war who had been captured at Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I'm almost certain he told me that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would agree that he was a professional military man, in the military all his professional life, and a former Yugoslav National Army officer?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You found Colonel Blaskic to have a dominant personality, I believe, and you've described him as a hard man; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I found him a straightforward, military man with a strong character but whom I had considerable respect for as a professional soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You spoke the same language essentially, in professional terms, not linguistic terms, as Colonel Blaskic; would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is a perfectly fair assessment of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I believe you said earlier, General, that you found him to be reliable, except for one occasion.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on that, if it is something that --

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I can. I can. During the crisis in January when the road at Kacuni got cut, Busovaca was effectively cut off and we could get no supplies to it or through it. Therefore, there was a large population that were very short of food, and we were in mid winter in Bosnia. Colonel Blaskic came to see me and asked if a number of trucks, and I think it was three or four, loaded with potatoes that were being brought up from Mostar, if I was to escort them through into Busovaca as the U.N., as his people were starving in Busovaca. I said I would but then gave directions that the potatoes on these trucks were to be offloaded and placed into British -- sorry, I apologise, into Dutch U.N. transports to take them through. This caused a certain amount of consternation with Colonel Blaskic and his staff, but we did unload them and reload them. I can't remember the exact tally that we found on these trucks, but it was many thousands of rounds of ammunition, certainly seven RPG rockets, and a large number of hand grenades amongst the potatoes. That was the only occasion when Colonel Blaskic let me down in his dealings that I am aware of, but that was the occasion I was referring to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In your statement, on page 6, you describe Colonel Blaskic as a -- you say: "He had a dominant personality, a hard man." Do you still subscribe to those views or --

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: There was a very serious civil war or war at this stage throughout Bosnia. A great number of people were being killed, a great number of people were being driven out of their homes, entire law and order had broken down throughout the country, and Colonel Blaskic was a military commander with a large Croat population in his area of responsibility. Inevitably, he had to be hard in some of the decisions that he took.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would agree with me that Colonel Blaskic was facing a situation of military, social, ethnic crisis effectively at that time and that he bore a very heavy burden of responsibility in his area of responsibility; would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I think the situation was extremely grave, and he was a military commander in the area and faced, as we all did, some pretty unpleasant scenes and situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Did you find Colonel Blaskic to demonstrate a detailed understanding of military matters, military affairs?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn to the next subject, Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic. I understand that he was Colonel Blaskic's commanding officer, sir?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That was certainly the total impression I had throughout my time in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You have described Brigadier Petkovic as "definitely the commander of the entire HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That was the impression that he would have led us to believe certainly on my very few meetings with him when he came to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I understand that his headquarters were actually in the town of Mostar, which was heavily besieged by Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That town was being shelled on a relatively -- well, a regular basis by the Bosnian Serb artillery?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Mostar was in a terrible state by this time of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think that you have previously stated that Brigadier Petkovic did not normally attend MMWG meetings?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Except when General Morillon wished to chair them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When he did attend a meeting, you tried to ensure that General Morillon would also be in attendance, effectively as his equal, if you wish?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That's not correct. If General Morillon called a Mixed Military Working Group which he intended to chair, which happened on at least two occasions, I would ensure that General Petkovic was present as the person responsible at that level, rather than the other way around, which is the way I think your question was posed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: My question was based upon page 6 of your statement, sir, if you would just take a look at that and look at the third full paragraph down, beginning "Petkovic"?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, but what you're referring to here is not necessarily a Mixed Military Working Group. I did have one -- two or three meetings with Petkovic. These were arranged by appointment. This is when Petkovic would come to the headquarters, as opposed to a Mixed Military Working Group in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Perhaps we're not speaking about --

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: On those occasions, I would ask, where appropriate, if General Morillon would come up from Sarajevo to Kiseljak, because, of course, Petkovic would not normally go into Sarajevo because of the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you did not ask General Morillon to attend meetings with either Colonel Blaskic or Mr. Kordic, I take it?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Apart from the meeting on the 1st of February, the answer is no. I normally -- in fact, I dealt with them myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that you actually received written protests from Brigadier Petkovic regarding ceasefire violations?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I'm sure I did. I received more protests from more people about more ceasefire violations in six months than could fill chapters of books.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just show you one of your replies to apparently a ceasefire violation protest by Brigadier Petkovic, and I'll pass very briefly over this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D69/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm drawing your attention to this exhibit. Is this a letter that you wrote on the 12th of November, 1992 back to Brigadier Petkovic, the chief of staff of the HVO in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would just like to turn to the final topics of questions that I have for you, sir, and I hope to be finished in about ten or fifteen minutes. Would it be fair to say that you did not find the views or positions that were articulated by Mr. Kordic, in whatever meetings that he had with you at the end of 1992, to be hard line or strident?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: At that stage, I would agree with that statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever seen any press conferences or public interviews that may have been televised or broadcast over the radio in which Mr. Kordic ever exhibited or articulated extreme or hard line views, that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It was clear to you, General, when you met Mr. Kordic that this was not a military man; would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I think that would be a fair assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He described to you, quite candidly, his journalistic background before the civil war broke out, I take it?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Very candidly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And admitted to you that he had absolutely no military background, no effective military training?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Does it seem logical to you, General, that a non-military man would be in military command or co-command of an army that was made up, at its highest levels, of professional soldiers with extensive, professional military backgrounds in the JNA, such as Colonel Blaskic or Brigadier Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It doesn't seem logical that someone who is untrained in military affairs should have a military position, as opposed to a politician having overall control of the military as in any normal democracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Would it be fair to say that you did not personally dislike Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That would be fair to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you find the views that he articulated regarding concerns for his fellow Croats at any time to be less than completely genuine?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No. I think that his position was what I would have expected of someone trying to look after his own population in the middle of what was a very evil civil war that was raging.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would agree that each side here was looking out or trying to look out for its own best interests and trying to protect, to the best of its ability, the civilian population that was threatened with death and destruction during the middle of this vicious, internecine civil war?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, but with a slight outlook as to who could get the advantage out of any peace process that subsequently came along.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But that's the nature of peace negotiations, General, wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn to the title of "Colonel" in connection with Mr. Kordic. I believe you gave some testimony about that. You stated, I believe, that it was your conclusion that it was necessary for Mr. Kordic to have the rank of Colonel in order to ensure that he was not subordinate to Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That was my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, would it be fair to say that as to Colonel Blaskic's rank, you were in absolutely no doubt whatsoever? He was a Colonel, he looked like a Colonel, he talked like a Colonel, he was a military man?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In connection with the journalist-cum-politician Kordic, did he actually wear any rank insignia that you could see?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I regret that after all these years I can't now remember whether he did wear insignia, but all I do recall is that he definitely introduced himself as Colonel Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you remember him wearing rosary beads and a crucifix?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, it's true, sir, that throughout the time that you dealt with these three gentlemen, Brigadier Petkovic, Colonel Blaskic, and Mr. Kordic, you weren't sure about the relationship between Mr. Kordic and Colonel Blaskic specifically, were you?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Not absolutely certain, no, except that at the Mixed Military Working Group, I think on the 28th of November, he definitely introduced himself in front of the Serb delegation and the ABiH Presidency Forces delegation as the man responsible for the HVO at the Mixed Military Working Group, and since Colonel Blaskic was present at the same meeting and didn't demur in any way at all, I assume that, therefore, he was taking a position of superior to Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I understand that that was your assumption, General, but did Colonel Blaskic ever tell you that he was subordinate to the military or political authority of Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did General -- I'm sorry. Did Brigadier Petkovic ever tell you that Mr. Kordic was superior in authority to Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No. Except the one meeting where he said that the implementation of a certain agreement would be undertaken by Colonel Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One final question on this subject. It would be fair to say, just in general terms, that between you on the one hand and the Croat delegation on the other, there simply was no discussion of the relative hierarchy or military position of the people within that delegation, was there?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I never asked the direct question. Provided someone delivered the goods, I was happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And no one ever actually told you, volunteered the information regarding the relative rankings or purviews of each one of those representatives of the delegation, did they?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Other than in the ways that I have described.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would agree, sir, that Colonel Blaskic seemed to you always to be able to deliver on any military commitments or decisions that he made; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Once he had agreed, yes, he could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You found it more uncertain to be able to expect commitments made by Mr. Kordic to be carried out, is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: To a degree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, turning to the subject of the involvement of Croatian military units in Central Bosnia, would it be fair to say that you only heard rumours of HV troops operating specifically in the areas of Gornji Vakuf and Mostar in December of 1992 and January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Absolutely. I have no -- I never had any hard substantiated evidence of these claims which were almost constant from both the ABiH and more from the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In connection with this, just two questions. You never saw any HV troops yourself throughout your tour in the Kiseljak valley, did you?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: The answer is no, because so many people looked so similar in those things, and all you have to do is remove one flash and put a different flash on to change your allegiance. The answer, therefore, is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. On a more general level, did you find, in your five months in Central Bosnia, that it was routine for fanciful claims to be made on the part of each one of the three competent ethnic factions?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Without any doubt, yes, and exaggeration was all part of the game for propaganda reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: General Cordy-Simpson, thank you very much indeed. You have been an excellent witness. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. President. I only have one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: General Cordy-Simpson, would you be kind enough to tell us were there ever in your meetings with representatives of Herceg-Bosna, the HVO, or any other Croatian entity in Bosnia, whether you ever met a person called Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I have no recollection of meeting Mario Cerkez, but then I met an awful lot of people in some fairly strange circumstances during my tour of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) That's all I have for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, a few matters, but first, dealing with the 1st February meeting with Kordic and others for which we haven't at the moment got a document, are there any records available to you that you've been able to consult that deal with that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, insofar as I did keep a private diary, and hence why I knew the 1st of February as a date, that it was General Morillon's promotion date and that he came through the headquarters from Sarajevo. On his way through we briefed him up on what was required before he went on his way up to Vitez to chair this meeting, and everything that I subsequently remember of that meeting in Vitez, which after the one that was being referred to by the Defence, both Blaskic and Kordic were present, but as I said, I wasn't. I set up the meeting. But I'm sure if he hadn't been present, I would have recorded something to the fact that he hadn't shown up, but I may be absolutely wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been able to consult your notes before giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your private diary?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, we've seen a letter from you to Petkovic, coming from some source, but would there be any other document identifying the details of the 1st of February meeting existing in somebody's archives, the HVO's or somebody else's?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Well, there absolutely has to be. There has to be within the U.N. They are almost certainly within the 1st Battalion of the Cheshire's battle group. Their war diary will reflect that that meeting took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll try and turn that up, but equally, in your experience, would it exist within the records of the other interested parties, such as a document?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I would be almost certain that both the ABiH and the HVO would have kept a record of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's suggested to you that there was nobody that volunteered the comparative ranking of individuals, that is, Blaskic, Kordic, and others. As we know, at the meeting on the 28th of November, matters were spelled out specifically that he was the chairman and the superior of Colonel Blaskic. Was it ever necessary for that matter to be revisited?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No, because subsequently Colonel Kordic, having made his statement, always attended the Mixed Military Working Groups, when they were called, as the HVO representative, with the exception of the time of the 7th of December, I think it is, when he did not turn up but sent me a fax to say that he wasn't going to turn up once the meeting had more or less started.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Everything that happened subsequent to that, did it in any way support or in any way displace the judgement that you made on the basis of what was said to you about the comparative positions of people?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No. I took it, and no one ever contradicted it in the HVO circles, that Kordic was the man to whom I was to deal as the leader of the HVO delegation for the Mixed Military Working Group, and certainly subsequently, whenever we sent out an invitation to the next Mixed Military Working Group, including the necessary arrangements for escorts, flags of truce, et cetera, to cross the confrontation lines, we would have sent them to Colonel Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as to your opinion that authority was delegated to him for Central Bosnia of which you spoke, was there anything that was said or anything that happened that ran counter to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Nothing ran contrary to that assumption that I had made and had been led to believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked a little further about the difficulty of getting Kordic to deliver in comparison with the position so far as Blaskic is concerned. Can you just amplify on that. Are you speaking of his ability or his intention? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I -- probably both. From his ability, it would be a fact that as a non-military man, he may have found it harder to understand my military intentions. He, in turn, may have found it harder to pass it on as clear military orders. As for his intentions, as I have said, I initially found him helpful and genuinely concerned for the Croat population. As things rapidly deteriorated in January, I found -- as I found with most of the Croat population, it harder to achieve what we were, the United Nations, trying to achieve, which was trying to stop the breakdown of complete law and order into utter anarchy in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because you've been asked about your views about him at the time. Following from your last answer, when you first encountered him and first formed these views, these first views, what was the general position of the Croats in comparison to the position of others? What, if anything, did they have at that stage to gain or lose from cooperation with you?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: The Croats, for really almost the first time, were facing a very serious situation inside Sarajevo, which was at that stage completely dominant in their thought process. There was one of the very worst situations that I remember in Sarajevo. We're not just talking of the odd shell, we are talking of a city completely surrounded; no water; no electricity; no fuel; no heating of any form, shape, or size; with anything of up to a thousand rounds of mortar or artillery impacting in a single day into the town; large numbers being killed; and the Serbs launching an offensive out of the Ilidza area, which is on the western side of Sarajevo forward to the Stup area of Sarajevo, which takes in a large part of Sarajevo which was inhabited by Croat civilians who were now in a very precarious situation. Against that background, I believe that Colonel Kordic saw in us, the United Nations, a chance to relieve some of the suffering by getting these people out of Sarajevo if I could possibly achieve it. In January, of course, the situation did change somewhat with the breakdown of the comparatively weak alliance between the ABiH and the HVO in Central Bosnia, and from my own perspective, purely as a military man, this linked itself fairly closely with the peace process that was developing in Geneva where the Vance-Owen Plan was being developed and quite a lot of people were intent on grabbing what they could before something was finally signed in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did your views, your initial views, in any degree change as events unfolded?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I suppose in some ways they did, insofar as the war in Central Bosnia got worse up to the 1st of February, by which time effectively Geneva had failed and some form of peace agreement was -- temporary peace agreement was desperately needed for breathing space in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The grabbing of what might have come at Geneva, how was that reflected so far as the Croat side was concerned?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: A huge amount of illegal checkpoints were thrown up, and there was a great deal of burning of houses, both Muslim and Croat, I have to say, and very severe fighting between the Muslims and the Croats in particularly Gornji Vakuf, where the town was a mixed population town and divided itself almost straight down the road that ran through the town itself, one side fighting against the other side and the place becoming a complete no-go area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's now five past one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I've very nearly finish. If you can allow me a couple more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Obviously if it was possible over the adjournment to find any further document dealing with the 1st of February I'd ask the witness to stay behind, but that apart -- and I don't think it's going to be fine or possible because we've searched our materials already. Then I'll be able to complete him in about a couple of minutes if that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Serbs and Muslims were engaged against each other where?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: The Serbs and the Muslims, at this stage in December, throughout whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, right the way round what was then to eventually solidify as to what is known as the confrontation line, and this went right down through Mostar, all the way round Sarajevo, all the way up through towards Tuzla, back round just north of Vitez and then linking back down towards Mostar itself again from the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That did not involve the Croats, but the question is: What did that do, if anything, in your judgement, for the ability of Croats and, in particular, of Colonel Kordic to be cooperative and express cooperative views?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Well, insofar as they were not being directly threatened and, therefore, hadn't a particular problem, they could afford to be slightly generous, I suspect, in their cooperation with UNPROFOR to appear to be helpful to us insofar as at this stage they weren't being threatened. But of course, subsequently, in December, in the middle of Sarajevo and then again in January in Central Bosnia, that position changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The decline in conditions, did that link in time at all with the development of the Mixed Military Working Group meetings and with Colonel Kordic's arrival at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I couldn't say that that would be a direct reflection. Colonel Kordic arrived on the 28th of November. The Serb offensive into Central Sarajevo happened in the beginning of December, which put the Croats in such a difficult position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last two questions. The Mixed Military Working Group of the 22nd of December, you've been asked certain questions about David Pinder's notes and material. What would you say to a suggestion that at that meeting, the 22nd of December, all the work had previously been done by Kordic and Guervo and, therefore, the meeting was for the two senior commanding Generals to sign what had been worked out?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That would be a fair assessment, because inevitably, before we brought together Mladic, or Petkovic, any of the senior commanders, with Morillon in the chair, we would only do it if we felt that we had some chance of getting a successful conclusion and signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last question. You've spoken right at an early stage of the cross-examination of his role as vice-president of something. Can you remember now how he, in fact, introduced himself to you at either the first or an early meeting?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Well, I am almost certain that on my meeting with him on the 12th of December, 1992, he introduced himself as the Deputy President of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm almost certain that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That concludes my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. As far as the Court's concerned, you are released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to go now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, we've made good progress today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Akhavan, although he's had to be at a hospital this morning, I think that his wife is -- something like that, is back this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We should conclude his cross-examination then this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. What about tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I regret I haven't been able to whistle up, in the vernacular, another witness at short notice for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Once we finish Mr. Akhavan, it does -- it does mean that we have time, and if necessary, we'll do it tomorrow, to have the Status Conference which we discussed. I think it's important that we review the position. We'll see how we get on. I would, in particular, want to look at the witness list again, in light of the progress made, and see what can be done about it. You've got the decision on the dossier now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It's all in hand, and I'll have a list of witnesses probably, I think, to take us through to the end of the sittings in the autumn, depending on the speed we achieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll consider those matters later. We'll sit again at quarter to three. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.15 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General Cordy-Simpson had been rescheduled to depart from the hotel immediately opposite the building at 3.00, but meanwhile, he researched his notes and revealed to me that, contrary to his belief, Kordic is not mentioned as having been present at the meeting on the 1st of February. The notes only refer to Morillon and unidentified two leaders of the brigades. He can't account for how the paragraph appears in page 5 of his statement, and it hasn't been possible at the moment to disinter any other document that may have supported that assertion. The only other documents, of which I am aware, of the invitation that was sent to Kordic the day before and which has already been produced in evidence, but I think that the milinfosum itself for the day in question will again only name Morillon, Blaskic, and the others. So the position is that, in the absence of any further material, we won't be inviting you to -- in the absence of any further evidence or written material, we wouldn't be inviting you to conclude that Kordic was present at that meeting. General Cordy-Simpson extends, of course, his apologies for getting something wrong. He suspects that the error arises from misrecollecting what was in the witness statement as being in his own diary. I had to make a decision whether it was necessary to bring him back, further to put off his flight, or to relate to you and to the Defence the information that I've got. I judged that since we'd be saying, "Absent further documentation, we won't be arguing his presence on the 1st of February," all parties would be happy for him to return to England.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. It seems to be a sensible outcome. There's no need for the General to apologise for a misrecollection after all this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely. Can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you would forward the Court's thanks for his putting the matter right for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will certainly do that. I've, of course, expressed our own gratitude for that. The only other thing I might as well do now before we part from his evidence, although again it doesn't need his attendance, is there was a question about document 336.1 -- sorry, yes, document 336.1, which, as the Court will remember, refers on its face to two meetings but contains only supporting material for one meeting, and, indeed, the Court may have noticed that there was some suggestion that there was another document that had got detached or hadn't been printed, because the third to last page of that document, as provided to you, reads "13/" and it's pretty clear that the "/" was "18." I have been able to have printed out the sequential page numbers according to the registry's, or whatever the system is, numbering. If I can distribute this, please, three for the Judges and two for the Defence, I will keep one for myself and hand it in in a minute -- I've got another one here. This should be, so that it conforms in general format with the way the other documents have been produced, this should simply become part of 336.1, so it doesn't need a separate number. It deals with the 26th of December meeting, and one can see straightaway that the participants were by different names and at a lower level than the other meetings we've been concerned with, and, I think, simply putting it shortly, it's pretty non-consequential. But it's there for completeness in case anybody wants to see it, and I hope that helps. May Mr. Akhavan come back, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Akhavan.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We will try to be concluded with your cross-examination, at least from the perspective of Mr. Kordic, by 3.45, if possible. Let me draw your attention to the events of April the 15th, 1993. You are aware, are you not, that Commander Zivko Totic of the Jure Francetic Brigade in Zenica was kidnapped, and three of his bodyguards were executed in a hail of gunfire, which also resulted in the death of one civilian passer-by; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that's in my notes. I'm not sure if you're referring to the exact same events. I do recall a kidnapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Did Colonel Stewart tell you, during the briefing that you say you received from him connected with the events of April the 15th and 16th at Ahmici and elsewhere, that the Totic kidnapping was an extremely serious, indeed, inflammatory incident that could cause the entire Lasva Valley to explode in vicious inter-ethnic fighting?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think my notes reflect what I was told, and it indicates that, indeed, it was a serious incident. However, it was part of a buildup of tensions and not an isolated event.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You are aware that the Totic kidnapping was preceded by a day or two by an incident in which four HVO officers were captured assertedly at the hands of the 7th Muslim Brigade outside of the town of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it's in my notes: "Muslims kidnapped four HVO staff officers from Novi Travnik."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You're also aware that the 7th Muslim Brigade was responsible for the kidnapping of Commander Totic?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is the HVO brigade commander from Travnik that you refer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: From Zenica, sir.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I have that. In any event, I have reports of several incidents of kidnapping of HVO members by the Bosnian Muslim forces in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did Colonel Stewart brief you that these events could be the catalyst for some serious inter-ethnic fighting?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: If what you are suggesting is that that was the cause and the effect was the ethnic cleansing of Muslims in the Lasva Valley region, I don't believe that anyone suggested that. But if you're suggesting that it would give rise to tensions of a military character, yes, I believe that all sides believed that this was part of a buildup of tensions over several months which had involved a series of retaliations between Bosnian Croat and Bosnian Muslim forces against one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So Colonel Stewart did brief you that these events could be the catalyst for some serious inter-ethnic fighting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It depends on what you mean by "inter-ethnic fighting". If you mean the slaughter of civilians, I'm not sure if that is what their explanation would be. But if you mean exchanges, military exchanges between the Bosnian Croat and Muslim forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you two milinfosums prepared by the 1st Cheshire Regiment, if I may. The first one is milinfosum 166, dated April the 14th, 1993 and the second one is milinfosum 167, dated April the 15th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The documents are marked D70/1 and D71/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Usher, I have a second set of documents here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, these documents need not detain us long. If I could turn your attention to milinfosum 166, April 14, 1993. I'd just like you to look at page 2, please. This milinfosum describes the abduction of four HVO officers in Novi Travnik by the 7th Muslim Brigade. Have you ever seen this milinfosum before?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I looked through a number of milinfosums while I was there, but the information contained here is already in my handwritten notes more or less, but I'm not sure if I saw this particular milinfosum. I have the information, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Turning to the second milinfosum, number 167, dated April the 15th, 1993, I would like to draw your attention to two sections. First on page 1, section 2, entitled "Vitez", and secondly on page 2, section 5, entitled "Zenica". Turning to the Vitez entry first, were you informed that two ABiH soldiers had been abducted assertedly by HVO forces in the town of Vitez on the night of April the 15th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall specifically, but I was told that abduction was something that both sides engaged in from time to time. I'm not sure about this particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You did speak to the commander of the 325th Brigade detachment in Vitez, Sefkija Dzidic; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean of the Bosnian government forces? I met -- the name does not sound familiar. I did meet some representative of the Bosnian army. I'm not sure if it's that particular individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware that two ABiH soldiers had been abducted in Vitez on the night of April the 15th?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I mentioned previously, I was informed in general terms about such abductions. I'm not sure about this particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that Sefkija Dzidic and also Ramiz Dugalic, the deputy commander of the 325th Brigade, had stated that if the release of the two BiH soldiers did not happen soon, the situation in Vitez would deteriorate rapidly?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that. I do have in my notes, however, that the HVO made similar threats. So it seemed to be part of the communication pattern between the two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Turning your attention to the second page, up at the top there, were you briefed by any of the British soldiers that accompanied you that if these two BiH soldiers had not been returned soon, then some form of retaliatory action by the BiH against HVO is highly likely?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Were we told when, on --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were briefed, along these lines, by the British soldiers from whom you say you received the briefing on the 30th of April or at any time thereafter.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, in response to your question, I would refer you to page 2 of my handwritten notes. At the bottom of the page, the second last sentence, which I think captures what we were interested in, that: "The conflicts were not new but the atrocities were unprecedented. We were told that there had been tensions between the Bosnian Croats and Muslims for quite some time, dating back even to 1992, and that there had been kidnappings and killings."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, that is a simple question. It deals with the abduction of the two BiH soldiers and the threat of retaliatory action. It does not require you to repeat the opinions that you have given repeatedly over the course of the last few days. The question has a narrow focus. It's very simple. Were you or were you not told that in the evaluation of the British army, if the two BiH soldiers were not returned soon, on the evening of the 15th of April, then a retaliatory action by the BiH against the HVO was highly likely, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but the way you asked the question makes it seems as if I was there prior to April the 16th, but in retrospect, if you're saying that they suggested to me that the abductions may have been the catalyst for the armed conflict, no, that was not -- no one suggested to me that that was the catalyst for the wide-spread violence that took place from April 16th onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Turning to the Zenica entry on this milinfosum, were you aware that the 7th Muslim Brigade had, in fact, been responsible for the abduction of Commander Totic and the execution of his guards?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I think we've gone through this before, and my notes, once again, on page 3 of my handwritten notes, indicates facts which, frankly speaking, were not directly relevant to our inquiry but they indicate several cases of abduction. Whether the case which you particularly refer to time and again is included here, I'm not sure. We have: "Muslims kidnapped four HVO staff officers from Novi Travnik. We have also kidnapped HVO brigade commander from Travnik, 7th Muslim Brigade. The kidnapping was blamed on the 7th Brigade units. BritBat received notice that ten HVO people are hostages in exchange for Muslims in Busovaca prison." That gave us an overall sense that both sides were abducting and using people as hostages to exchange for hostages taken by the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever see the hostage note received by the ECMM from these gentlemen in Zenica, the abductors of Commander Totic?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure. We looked through many, many documents. We were there. I cannot instantly recollect having seen that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could be shown Exhibit D26/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, the usher has kindly placed upon the ELMO the ransom note or the extortion note to which I earlier referred. Have you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It does not look familiar, but as I said, it's very difficult for me to recollect. We went through several hundred pages of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If it does not look familiar to you, sir, let's move on. Turning to the subject of Lieutenant-Colonel Bob Stewart. Did Colonel Stewart brief you that Colonel Blaskic was the overall HVO military commander in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: So yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Kordic has any kind of a military background at all, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not aware whether he has military background or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I take it that during your 15-minute exchange with Mr. Kordic, the subject of his military credentials did not crop up?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Frankly speaking, what I had prior to the meeting, in several exchanges, and I draw your attention to page 2 of my handwritten notes, in the middle, the description of Dario Kordic being, "Mate Boban's right-hand man. Implements policy of Boban, head of HDZ for Central Bosnia. Input into all HVO brigades in Central Bosnia. Kordic gives political direction to Blaskic. He gets openly involved in political matters, especially in Busovaca area."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: So I was not--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment while we're dealing with that passage. Mr. Akhavan, what is the passage referring to or, rather, what is the source of the information that's being referred to there?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I can draw your attention to the top that has a page which says: "Overview of events, BritBat, 30 April," I believe that was the evening -- that's the evening when we arrived in Vitez. That is, several members of the British Battalion, I think maybe three, four, possibly five individuals, including Bob Stewart, to the best of my recollection, gave us an overview of Central Bosnia, the key actors, the tensions which existed between the Muslims and Croats. That was the general description which we received of Dario Kordic as one of the most influential actors in the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were never briefed in any way that Dario Kordic was any sort of a military commander, were you, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. We were told that he does get involved in military matters, but we were not told that he is a military commander as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were told, in fact, that his background was as a journalist before the civil war; right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: What we were told is that the HDZ and the HVO for the most part were quite inseparable, and that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: His background, sir. His background as a journalist before the civil war, you were told about that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall what his background was. Actually, maybe someone did say something to that effect, but there are two separate points here. One is whether he has a military background, the other is whether he gets involved in --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's not a question involved --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish. Yes, Mr. Akhavan?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, in terms of whether he has military training or not, I don't know. I do remember in the former Yugoslavia that there was compulsory service. I'm not sure if Mr. Kordic went through such service, but in any event, what was clear is that the political aspect of the Herceg-Bosna government, the HDZ mainly, which was, frankly speaking, the party with any power, was constantly in all aspects of decision-making, including military policy in the broad sense. If you're saying that he was involved in the day-to-day combat operations, no. That would fall into the hands of someone such as Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What you've just said; how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, this is based on what everyone in the region that I spoke with said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In other words --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The members of the British Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- you're just relating what you were told by other people?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me read you a page or passage from Colonel Stewart's book, on page 298, where he relates how he discovered what had happened at Ahmici. "Over the next two weeks or so, the facts about what had happened at Ahmici started to come out. My main sources were Thomas Osorio and Payam Akhavan, both members of the U.N. Centre for Human Rights." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he's speaking about the facts of what happened in the village of Ahmici in terms of how the atrocities were carried out, but I don't think he's suggesting that having spent several months there patrolling the region on a daily basis, that we came from the outside and told him about the overall situation in the region. It is true because Colonel Stewart was not qualified as an investigator, as a lawyer, as someone who does human rights investigations, that he would not nor would any of his soldiers conduct such an investigation. So he did rely upon us for the detailed accounts of how the events in Ahmici would have transpired and what the legal implications would be thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Let's turn for a minute to your draft report, the document that I believe has been marked as D66/1. Now, sir, did I understand you to say earlier that you drafted this interim report?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You concede, I believe, on the first page, that the main supply routes -- this is in paragraph 3: "The main transport routes" as you describe them, "in Central Bosnia are of great strategic significance, and control of them formed a source of great tension between the various competent factions in the region"?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On page 4 of your interim report, at paragraph 11, you describe armed clashes between the Bosnian army and the HVO in Vitez on the morning of April the 16th, and you report that these events quickly spilled over into the town and surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Are you familiar or have you ever read a United Nations document entitled "Final Report of the United Nations Commission of Experts Established Pursuant to Security Council Resolution 780, Annex 3(A) Special Forces," and the date of that report is December the 28th, 1994?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've read the report itself. I'm not sure that I've read the annex which you're referring to, but I believe that the report would have a summary of the annex probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Indeed, it does. It has a summary of reported paramilitary activity in Zenica and the surrounding area, and let me just read you a passage from this and see if you agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Copies, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Just for the Court's information, this is an extremely extensive document, probably four inches thick. I have excepted the portions of it that are of interest to this examination. If the Court wishes the entire document to be made an exhibit, I'd be more than happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the excerpts be the exhibit for the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D72/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: For everybody's easy reference and in the interest of expediency, I have underlined the areas of these excerpts of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On the first page, one excerpt says: "In the 21st of October, 1992 attack on Vitez, the Green Berets reportedly acted under the command of MTD and their commander, Rasim Delic." Were you aware of that attack on Vitez on October the 21st, 1992 by special forces?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is more than a year before the events in Ahmici. I think it would have hardly concerned us --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Then let's move on --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: -- in this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- Mr. Akhavan, to the fourth page, I believe, that says: "Allegations of war crimes," subparagraph E, and the lines that I have underlined say as follows: "It was reported that a unit of the Mujahedin called the Guerilla participated in the 16th of April, 1993 attack on Vitez and attempted to exchange ten HVO hostages for foreign prisoners held in HVO prisons."

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you disagree with this statement contained in an otherwise apparently authoritative United Nations document, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I mean, specifically, I cannot disagree with it in the sense that my own notes reflect that the Mujahedin were present in the region, and, as I said on page 3 of my notes, I did note down that ten HVO people were held as hostages in order to exchange them for Muslims kept in Busovaca prison. This specific participation on the 16th of April, I cannot confirm or deny, but it would seem to be credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Just turning briefly over some other parts of your draft report, you record, on page 6, in paragraph 17, that there was no evidence of any HOS involvement in the attack upon Ahmici insofar as the circumstances of that attack were related to you by eyewitnesses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that sentence should be read as saying that the HVO, for the most part, were responsible for the atrocities, not to say that it is inconceivable that HOS had any participation. We were told that HOS did not exist in significant numbers in the region, Mr. Kordic himself told me that, at most, there would be 100 HOS in the region, and the attack on Ahmici and Vitez, if one puts it all together, it would have required several hundred armed forces. That alone, in addition to the testimony of witnesses and others, suggested that the HVO and not HOS, for the most part, was responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and thank you for that, but it is true that you and your colleague, throughout your one-week of investigation and interviews, received not a single report that any individuals in distinctive black uniforms were seen participating in the incidents and events at Ahmici; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: We did not receive such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, on page 18 -- sorry, page 7, and there may be some transposed pages in the report because that's how we got it from the OTP, but paragraph 18 contains some references to political figures in the region continuously using the media as a means of demonising other ethnic groups. Did you, in your one-week of investigations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you found that, Mr. Akhavan? Have you that passage?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think it's found at the bottom of page 6, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you yourself see any videotapes of news broadcasts or press conferences in which these leading political figures had made any statements?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not, which is why the report says, "It was pointed out to the team," as opposed to "the team saw for itself."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you hear any audiotapes of news broadcasts or political party broadcasts or press conference broadcasts in which these leading political figures had made these demonising type of comments?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you yourself read any newspaper articles that contained reports of such press conferences or speeches during which these demonising sorts of invective, which you have described, appear?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. This was based entirely on what local -- I should say, international forces and agencies in the region had to tell us, including those who understood Serbo-Croatian and could follow the local media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did the British soldiers who you had talked with say that they had seen any such videotapes, heard any such radio broadcasts, or read any such newspaper articles?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot recollect at this point who it was that told us, but two or three people who did speak Serbo-Croatian did say that it was often the case that the media would include Mr. Dario Kordic making what they perceived as inflammatory speeches and that very often Mr. Blaskic was in his presence. It was not so much the written media. Most people told me about the television. I don't believe the radio was also included.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Names, please?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot recall at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Unattributed sources conveyed this information to you, I take it?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wouldn't call them unattributed sources. For the purpose of our report, all that we have done is say that it was pointed out to us. I think that is a fair description of the situation. Obviously, we did believe that the people that were saying it to us were not outright liars, that there was some credibility to what they were saying; otherwise, we wouldn't have bothered to include it. But we did, as a standard matter, say that it was pointed out or that it was alleged or that it was related to us that, from reliable sources. If something was unreliable, we would simply not include it. If we witnessed something ourselves or managed to conduct an investigation where we were convinced of the fact, then we would make a statement to the effect that we believed this to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you make a note of those reliable sources in your notes?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It may be -- I would have to -- I actually do think there are references to that, but I'm not sure exactly where they would be. But, of course, this was part of a much broader pattern. I don't think the Lasva Valley existed in isolation. We did monitor, for example, HTV in Zagreb on a regular basis, the coverage of Ahmici, for example, statements made by various officials, I believe, including Mr. Kordic on some occasions, interviews which he had on HTV, not to mention Defence Minister Susak, President Tudjman, and others, who almost systematically misinformed the public about the existence of any atrocities. I recall that there was no coverage of Ahmici in the main sort of television station for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Suffice it to say, sir, you cannot now identify who these supposedly reliable sources were, can you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I said, if I put that together with the fact that we did monitor the media in general, I think that they are relatively good sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You can't cite to us, and I don't want to beat a dead horse here, but you can't cite to us one name of a person who supposedly told you that they had seen such inflammatory, demonising types of political rhetoric, can you?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: If I was to go through my notes, make a few telephone calls, refresh my memory over six years, I probably could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just so the record is entirely clear, you never saw any such comments yourself?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did, after our visit in the Lasva Valley region, as I said, I monitored Zagreb Television regularly through colleagues of mine who were fluent in Serbo-Croatian, and if you look at subsequent reports which we submitted to the Human Rights Commission, you will see that we have entire sections on the role of the media. With respect to the particular accused, I do recall on subsequent occasions, after our investigation, having seen him on HTV making statements of one sort or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Which, of course, you couldn't understand because you don't speak the language?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Which I could understand through a competent translator, as you or anyone else would under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, turning to the annex to this document -- before we do that, though, one of the recommendations is, in paragraph 21, page 8 of my version, it may be page 7 of the version that you have, it says: "The signatories of the joint statement should be encouraged to immediately establish an independent commission in order to attribute individual responsibility for massive violations of human rights and to effectively punish the perpetrators."

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was that ever done?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Okay. Turning to the annex, what I would like to do is just focus on two things. First, page 13, paragraph 18 --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is in the annex?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Paragraph 18?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would agree that "The HVO commanders for Middle Bosnia and Vitez repeatedly confirmed to the team," as you've previously identified it, "that they are in full control of the area and that the HVO soldiers under their command could not engage in any military operation under any circumstances without explicit orders." That is, sir, an accurate reflection of what you were told during the course of your investigations, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Secondly, paragraph 19, I believe, should be of interest to the Trial Chamber. You say: "There is considerable evidence that prior to the attack on Ahmici, these political figures repeatedly used the media for advocacy of national and religious hatred that constitutes incitement to discrimination, hostility, and violence. The team gained the impression that such political figures may have considerably more influence in the decision-making process than the HVO military commanders."
