utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Paragraph 19 on page 13, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Paragraph 19?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We've put the number 13 on the bottom. There are two sets of documents here, Your Honour, and they both have consecutively numbered paragraphs, which is a little confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Yes. I do not have paragraph 19 on page 13. I have paragraph 20. It's not the conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It may be the preceding page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: The interim report? Are we speaking of the interim report?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. There's an annex to it, and it's paragraph 19 of the annex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got the annex? We don't have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Annex 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Paragraph 19 of annex 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: I think we have up to paragraph 16, and then we have the conclusions, paragraphs 20 to 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Perhaps I might put this on the ELMO so everybody can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for the confusion, Your Honour, but I believe that an accurate copy of that page is on the ELMO now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Once again, sir, this is your interim report, and you say that "There is considerable evidence that prior to the attack on Ahmici, these political figures repeatedly used the media for advocacy of national and religious hatred ..." and that that constituted incitement to discrimination. What was the considerable evidence?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I must say one thing, that what you're reading here is the report which we initially sent to Geneva about the information which we gathered in our visit. What happened is that this was submitted, let's say, May 7th or 8th, I'm not sure of the exact date, but soon after we came back, and the actual report that was officially circulated as a public document came out on May 19th. In that two-week period, many of the allegations which were involved here were checked and double checked. This was part of the procedure before we circulated the public document. But as I said, the considerable evidence, to the best of my recollection, were several individuals who spoke Serbo-Croatian, who followed the local media, and they were of the opinion, and this is not simply the opinion of one individual, we would rarely rely on the opinion of only one individual, several individuals who suggested that the accused, Dario Kordic, and, in certain cases, Colonel Blaskic by his side, had made all sorts of statements which they believed to be of an inflammatory character which distorted the truth, which involved misinformation. For example, the local media never, to the best of my knowledge, did any sort of coverage of the fact that the entire population of Ahmici, to give one example, was either killed or deported, that all of their homes were destroyed. The whole event was portrayed as an attack by the Mujahedin against Croats. The considerable evidence also includes, I must note, not only statements made by individuals such as Dario Kordic, but also people such as Defence Minister Susak who had visited, I believe, Travnik just around the time that the atrocities in Ahmici took place. So this is not exclusive to those who are involved in this particular case, because, once again, we were not involved in a criminal investigation against the accused in this particular case. We wanted to get a sense of what the authorities, the HDZ, which, of course, was very closely associated with Zagreb, was doing in order to create either a climate which was likely to create more self-restraint and tolerance in the population or which was likely to incite them to hatred and violence. Subsequent to this report, we covered very carefully, and prior to this report, coverage on HTV of the events, and as I said, it is fair to say that the coverage was exceptionally biased and distorted. So that, I believe, constitutes "considerable evidence".

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So you're telling us that considerable evidence consists not of what you've seen yourself with your own eyes and not what you've heard with your own ears but basically what you have been told by other people?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying. That is what you're saying. What I'm saying, for example, is that when I watched HTV in Zagreb prior to my trip to Ahmici and afterwards, the only thing that the television showed with respect to the Lasva Valley was a few Croatian mothers who were grieving -- who were aggrieved because their sons had been killed, for example, which of course is tragic, but not one television station showed anything about the extensive footage of the atrocities which had occurred in Ahmici. For example, CNN, BBC World, Sky News, ITN repeatedly showed pictures of the family of eight that had been burnt alive in their basement in Ahmici, of the mosque, the minaret which had been destroyed, not once did I see any coverage. This to me, is, objectively speaking, one-sided, biased reporting. Even if I cannot speak the language, the mere fact that the images do not even appear on television, I think would tell any man of average intelligence that this is not impartial coverage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So we're left with your conclusion that there was one-sided, biased reporting from the media that you actually saw in Zagreb, I believe. How do you know that there was no coverage, television coverage or radio coverage of the Ahmici incident actually in Central Bosnia, sir, in Zenica, Busovaca, or Vitez?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, in the same way that I was not in the village of Ahmici when people were being killed or burnt alive, but based on my conclusions on the testimony of others who happened to have been there and happened to have seen it. It's no different than any other sort of evidence, evidence in the context of a human rights report that one would find credible and reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, what is in paragraph 19, is that evidence before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: From what one of the Judges has said, I don't have confidence that it is, Your Honour. We need to check the materials that have been handed out to ensure that they're complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It seems to me that the purpose of your cross-examination here is more to test the credibility of the witness than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Not strictly speaking, Your Honour, with respect. It's really simply to point out to the Trial Chamber that the considerable evidence -- there really isn't any evidence. The witness never actually saw any evidence himself, and yet this appears to be -- this interim report and its successors appears to be the basis on which accusations have been levelled against the political figures associated with the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's why I say it goes to his creditability. I just wanted to say that in my own opinion, the whole line of cross-examination is a bit too argumentative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you should try to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I take the Court's point and I will move on swiftly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Turning to the actual written report of May the 19th, 1993, Mr. Akhavan --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sorry, could I have a copy of that report?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's Exhibit Z942. Prosecution Exhibit, May the 19th, 1993 report.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's it. Thank you. Yes, please. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You have stated, sir, that the only parts of this report that you prepared were paragraphs 38 through 44, I believe.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the only parts that I did draft?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's what I --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, quite the contrary. What I suggested is that what we would provide very often would be factual narratives. We would on occasion make recommendations or conclusions, but ultimately this report was that of the Special Rapporteur, and he decided, in particular, with respect to conclusions and recommendations, what to include. It would be more accurate to say that I was involved largely in, if you look at the cover page of the document, sections A, B, and C.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. Let me turn your attention to paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, as well as II, which involved executions by government forces in the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would agree that it was not possible to conduct an exhaustive investigation of all allegations; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is paragraph 2 you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you or the Special Rapporteur's conclusion was that there was a need for a further or further investigations to be carried out in a systematic way with the necessary personnel and resources; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether that was ever done?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: We did, in subsequent occasions, visit that region on several occasions. The situation can be best described as a field operation with exceptionally limited resources. At that time there were two of us covering all of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. At a later stage, our numbers increased to perhaps five, at most ten, several months later. In every case we would prioritise what we perceived to be particularly serious violations, and at the same time attempting to the extent possible to look at atrocities committed by both sides. I believe that after the events that we spoke about, most of our resources with respect to Herceg-Bosna were consumed by the events in Mostar, which became the focus of our investigations. Of course, at the same time there were the atrocities in the areas under Bosnian Serb control which also preoccupied us. So there was follow-up, in answer to your question in a general sense, but I'm not sure. We did visit that region again. I did not, but my colleagues visited that region at least two or three times afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, turning -- two final areas of inquiry, trying to meet my deadline which I see has arrived. The first is the Miletici investigation, and there is reference to milinfosum 177, dated April 25th, 1993, yesterday. I actually have that here. I've previously distributed a copy to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D73/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I could turn your attention, Mr. Akhavan, to the fourth page containing the sub-heading "For Miletici."

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Before we get to that, if you could look at the top of the page there. Let me just ask you if you were aware that the villages forming the HVO front line, as of April the 25th, 1993, consisted of -- or east of Dubravica were Pirici, Vidovici, Ahmici, and Loncari? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact names of the villages. What you're speaking about in terms of a front line was difficult to describe, because, for example, Stari Vitez was a pocket under Muslim control deep in the middle of areas under Croat control. So I'm not sure what you're referring to when you say "front lines." But we were aware that Zenica -- somewhere between Vitez and Zenica was the front line. I'm not sure how that would extend to the region around Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Turning to the Miletici incident, it's true, isn't it, that the village was surrounded by about 20 Muslim extremists who proceeded to round up the population and eject them from the village while keeping behind five military-aged young men?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: What we were told by the survivors, most of whom were elderly -- well, many of them were still there. I'm not sure if they were ejected right there and they wanted to leave because they feared that the forces may return and commit further atrocities, but there were at least still several residents there. Here we say in our report in paragraph 37: "Twenty-seven of the 34 inhabitants of the village are said to have left in fear for their lives." I don't recall what the number was of the Mujahedin who came to the village. It could have been 10, it could have been 20. That sounds realistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Take a look at page 15 of your notes.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of my handwritten notes? Page 15? I'm not sure if our page numberings are the same. What is on top of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It says: "Local Croats demanded to be moved by BritBat," at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's page 15 from the start. Excuse me while I find this. Yes. Yes, I found it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection as to how many soldiers invaded the village?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Approximately 20 people maximum, according to a local witness. As I said, it doesn't sound unreasonable to say that. There would have been that many people involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You actually went into one of the houses in Miletici yourself and found a cooking pot where one of the heads of the young Croat men had been found; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You saw this pot yourself; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There was still blood in it, along with a ladle; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You had been told that that young man's head had been cut slowly off, and that ladle had been used to baste his head with his own blood?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The next and final questions that I have for you concern the events in Ahmici. Were you shown any photographs of Muslim soldiers carrying sophisticated AKM automatic weapons, taken in Ahmici on the morning of April the 16th, 1993 by Lieutenant Matthew Wooley?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'll just point you to a portion of Lieutenant Wooley's statement taken two years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does the Lieutenant say that he told this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He does not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't take the matter any further then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do I understand you to be of the belief that the attack on Ahmici was completely unannounced, that it was a surprise attack, and that the village was undefended?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that most of the Muslim civilians in the village were completely caught by surprise. Yes, that is my belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you interview any soldiers who defended the village?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, from what I recall, many were yet to be found. I'm trying to think. Probably not. I don't think it was really possible for us at that point to find any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The final exhibit that I would like you to review, if you would --

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: We did, however, meet Muslim soldiers. I don't believe they were from Ahmici. We did meet Muslim soldiers. We did speak with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at Exhibit D13/2? This, sir, is a copy of the statement of Fuad Berbic taken for the Bosnia and Herzegovina presidency state commission for gathering facts on war crimes. Specifically I'd like you to turn, if you would, to page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been very liberal in the allowance of these sort of documents into evidence. Now, unless this witness has seen this document, it does not seem to be right to allow it into evidence. It may be that this is a witness, I don't know, who is going to give evidence. Have you seen this document, Mr. Akhavan?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I certainly do not think it should be exhibited. It shouldn't be at this stage. You can put to him a passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and that will conclude my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If this has been exhibited, delete it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we'll need to review these exhibits. Leave it for the moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me read to you two portions of this exhibit, on page 5. First: "On the eve of the 15 April attack, I was on guard duty. It was very quiet, dead calm. Our level of alertness had been increased by 50 per cent compared to the night before because unfamiliar uniformed persons had been seen. Ten men were on stand-by in the lower part of the village."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does this mean anything to you, Mr. Akhavan?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I believe, Your Honour, that the issue is whether the attack on the village of Ahmici was foreseen or not foreseen, and whether the Muslims probably put up a vigorous defence or whether they were caught completely by surprise. I believe that is what the question is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's what is being put. What is your answer to it?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN (Resumed)
utterances.text: My answer is that I don't believe that it is incredulous to say that there were tensions in the region and all men of military age carried some sort of weapon, whether sophisticated rifles or shotguns. But our impression, according to our report, is that the attack on the Muslims homes came so early in the morning that most or a significant number of people who were found dead were still barefoot, some of them in their pyjamas, suggesting that they had simply fled their homes very early in the morning, at the time of the morning call to prayer. I do not believe that Ahmici was a heavily fortified village or that the civilians were on alert, but it is true or possible that some of the local men who were bearing arms anticipated potential trouble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if the Court is taking a -- it's 4.00. Before the next cross-examination starts, there are three matters I want to raise, not just arising from the manner of the cross-examination of Mr. Sayers, and they are these: First, if -- and they arise because of experience with the way matters are argued by my friends opposite. First, if there are allegations to be put to this witness of bias or lack of good faith or lack of honesty, they better be put and they better be put clearly. I've noticed again a reference to the common employment of the witness with the Office of the Prosecutor, and it would be foolish of those opposite to think I'm sitting here not listening. Second and more fundamental as not just an oversight but an error of Mr. Sayers, I observed that they are seeking to adopt wholesale passages of the Blaskic defence. When challenged or asked why they were putting what Blaskic said, they said it was their case. Now, they know that in the Blaskic case, right at the last minute, a complete and comprehensive account of what actually happened in Ahmici was produced in the form after the dated document, I think, the 25th of May, the same time as the -- broadly, the examination of events by this witness. Now, as opposed to simply asking questions in a critical way, if they are going to adopt the Blaskic defence and this document which surfaced so late in the history of the Blaskic defence, then that is what should be being put to this witness to test his conclusions against their case. Third, because this witness is producing conclusions, if they are saying any of his conclusions are wrong, they should do so specifically and give him a chance to answer them. In my respectful submission, it would be appropriate for those cross-examining for Kordic to review those points that I've made and perhaps to put matters so that I can deal with them in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is this document that you're referring to, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The report that was produced, apparently a report on Ahmici by Sliskovic, produced on May the 25th, 1993, and produced in the very last minutes of Blaskic. Apparently it sets out what, from one perspective, is said to have happened. Now, if they're adopting the Blaskic defence, that will be their defence in this case, and it is incomprehensible to me that they would not be raising the factual matters alleged there. Of course, if they don't seek in any way to adopt what was put in Blaskic as a document of apparent record, however late in the day it surfaced and however long it remained wherever it all was, then that's all well and good, but that would still leave outstanding the conclusions that they say this witness should have reached different from the conclusions he did reach.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Robinson points out quite rightly you can put that in re-examination, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can deal with it, but I think, with respect, the Defence should be putting their questions quite clear on the topics which I've raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we have their case on Ahmici. I think it is to say, as I understand it, and I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, that they have no substantive case to put. They are testing the Prosecution evidence that the village was defended; there were Croat casualties; that they have no explanation, as far as I can understand, as to how the substantial Muslim casualties took place. Now, Mr. Sayers, does that accurately summarise your case on Ahmici or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you have summarised our position more tersely than we have. That is our position. There is no question that there were hostilities. I stress that there is no suggestion on the Defence's part that there was an attack by the Muslims themselves. It's quite clear that there were hostilities between HVO forces and some forces of whatever magnitude on the Muslim side in the village, that there were casualties on both the sides and that an atrocity was committed. That is our position. Why it is done, how it was done, we do not know, and I think I have made the position of the Defence clear before, and if I have not then I wish to make the position clear now, and that is this: Our client had nothing to do with it. But I think in terms of the matters of detail which you just recited, we would agree with all of them. That is indeed the Defence's position, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my dear colleague, Mr. Nice, just mentioned the document of May 25 entered recently in the Blaskic case, signed by Sliskovic, and, indeed, I was just preparing the questions for my cross of the witness, and I would like to use that document. Unfortunately, I was not able to get this document from the Blaskic case, up to this moment. I will get it probably in the next week or so. Could I kindly ask the Prosecutor to give me that document, since he has it and I've just heard about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, he can have a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll have to get him one. I haven't got it immediately, but I can get him one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Over the adjournment. Now, Mr. Kovacic, we have another ten minutes, quarter of an hour or so, which you might like usefully to use to begin your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may, of course, start, even though I would be glad to start tomorrow morning, because again we have a problem, some questions were taken by my dear colleague, Mr. Sayers, and perhaps I will fall into the mistake and repeat them. If I'm going through my notes this evening, I will be much more productive tomorrow morning. But whatever you decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long is your cross-examination to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I don't want to make any wrong forecast, but, with a certain tolerance, I think that I could get it in one hour, I'm sure. Your Honour, just with one small reserve: The witness obviously tends to evaluate things which counsel cannot expect, so please don't keep me to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One hour and a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning. When we've concluded the examination of the witness, we will have the Status Conference. I would like at that conference to look again at the overview of witnesses which you produced, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You will be letting us have an idea of whom you propose to call.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the time estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As far as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course. Yes, Mr. Stein?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: On that point, I've actually asked for, and I believe Mr. Nice will give us, a list of who he's going to call for the fall, September through December, in roughly the order he's going to call them, and we'll be asking for a more precise list for the first two weeks of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Any matters which you want to raise, Mr. Stein or Mr. Kovacic, tomorrow will be the time for us to take stock of how things have been going and to deal with any matters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I've actually sent a letter to Mr. Nice, and if Your Honour please, I will give you a copy. It lays out the issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, will you be back, please, at half past nine tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 4.10 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 5th day of August, 1999, at 9.30 a.m.
